[p. 137]

The basmalah (the formula "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") is a name for the phrase "bi-smi Allah." This name was formed from the letters of the two words (bi-smi) and (Allah) by a method called naht (coining a new word by blending parts of a longer phrase). Naht is the formation of a past-tense verb on the pattern fa'lala from the letters of a sentence or of a construct phrase. People use it to abbreviate a whole sentence when they want to make it lighter, because the phrase is so often on the tongue.

The Arabs used naht in forming relative adjectives (nisba) from a sentence or a compound when the nisba formed from its first or last part would be ambiguous. For example, for ʿAbd Shams they said ʿAbshamī, to avoid confusion with a nisba to ʿAbd or to Shams. For ʿAbd al-Dar they said ʿAbdarī in the same way, and for Hadramawt they said Hadramī. Sibawayh said in the chapter on iḍāfa, that is, on nisba to a construct noun: "They may make for the nisba in an iḍāfa a single name in the manner of Jaʿfarī, taking letters from the first and last parts and not removing them from their letters, so that it may be recognized." End of quotation. Later Arab muwallads (Arabic speakers born of non-Arab parents, or later generations) who came after them used this method for citing sentences that were very common on the tongue, for the sake of brevity. This began at the start of Islam, and so the method became an Arabic practice.

The poet al-Rāʿī said:

"A people upon Islam, who have not withheld their small kindnesses and have not neglected the tahlīl."

That is, they have not abandoned the saying "There is no god but Allah." ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:

"Layla said the basmala when I met her in the morning, ah, how lovely is that beloved who says the basmala!"

That is, she said "bi-smi Allah" out of fear of Him. The original root of basmala is the saying "bi-smi Allah." Then the muwallads applied it to the saying "bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm," relying on its fame, even though this coined form does not contain the ḥāʾ and the rāʾ, which are among the letters of al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm. So the saying "basmala" became common in the sense of saying "bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm." From the verb basmala a verbal noun, al-basmala, was derived, just as al-hayʿala was derived from hallala. This verbal noun is regular for the pattern fa'lala.

From this verb a active participle was derived in the verse of ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa, but no passive participle has been heard.

I saw in the commentary of Ibn Hārūn al-Tūnisī on the abridgement of Ibn al-Ḥājib, in the chapter on the adhān, citing al-Muṭarriz [p. 138] in his book "al-Yawāqīt": The verbs that were coined from their phrases are seven: basmala from "bi-smi Allah," sabḥala from "subḥān Allah," ḥayʿala from "ḥayya ʿalā al-ṣalāh," ḥawqala from "lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allah," ḥamdala from "al-ḥamdu li-Allah," hallala from "lā ilāha illā Allah," and jayʿala when one says "juʿiltu fidāka." He added ṭayqala from "aṭāla Allah baqāʾaka," and damʿaza from "adāma Allah ʿizzaka."

Since many imams of the religion hold that the basmala is a verse at the beginning of every surah except Barāʾa, or at the beginning of some surahs, it became necessary for the exegete to explain its meaning, its ruling, and its place, according to those who count it a verse from some surahs.

Discussion of it falls into three topics: the first concerns whether it is a verse at the beginning of the surahs or not; the second concerns the ruling on beginning with it when reciting; the third concerns explaining its specific meaning.

As for the first topic, there is no disagreement among Muslims that the words "bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm" are a Qur'anic expression, because they are part of a verse in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Naml: 30]. They also did not disagree that beginning important matters that have significance with the basmala was established in Islam. A ḥadīth was narrated on this: "Every matter of importance that does not begin with 'bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm' is cut off (abtar)." The authors of the Sunan did not narrate it, nor did the compilers of the Mustadrakāt. It has been described as ḥasan (good). The majority said that the scribes who wrote the copies of the Qur'an (maṣāḥif) wrote the basmala at the beginning of the surahs, except Surat Barāʾa, as is understood from the conversation of Ibn ʿAbbās with ʿUthmān, which passed in the Eighth Introduction. They did not disagree that it was written in the muṣḥaf at the beginning of Surat al-Fātiḥa, and that is not the place for separating one surah from what precedes it. They only disagreed about whether the basmala is a verse of Surat al-Fātiḥa and of the beginnings of the surahs other than Barāʾa. This means that their disagreement is not about whether it is Qur'an, but about whether its Qur'anic status is repeated, as Ibn Rushd al-Ḥafīd indicated in "al-Bidāya." Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, the jurists of Medina, Syria and Basra held that it is not a verse at the beginning of the surahs, but is part of a verse in Surat al-Naml. This is said with the exception of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr and Ibn Shihāb among the jurists of Medina. Al-Shāfiʿī in one of his two opinions, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, and the jurists of Mecca and Kufa, except Abū Ḥanīfa, held that it is a verse at the beginning of Surat al-Fātiḥa only. ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī in one of his two opinions, which is the more sound one from him, held that it is a verse of every surah.

No statement was transmitted from Abū Ḥanīfa among the jurists of Kufa about it. The author of al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī) understood from him that it is not one of the surahs in his view, so he counted him among those who said that it is not part of the surahs. This is the sound view from him. [p. 139] ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm said: This is because he held that it is not recited aloud with al-Fātiḥa in the prayers recited aloud, and he disliked reciting it at the beginnings of the surahs joined to al-Fātiḥa in the first two rakʿas.

I add and say: He did not regard limiting oneself to it in the prayer as sufficient in place of the recitation.

As for the argument of Mālik's school and those who agree with it, they have several approaches: one of them is through reasoning (naẓar), the second is through transmitted reports (athar), and the third is through Arabic linguistic sensibility (dhawq).

As for the first approach, the Mālikīs have an outstanding argument in this, from al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī. Ibn al-ʿArabī in "Aḥkām al-Qur'ān" and al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Wahhāb in "al-Ishrāf" followed him. Al-Bāqillānī said: If the basmala were part of the Qur'an, then the way to establish it would be either by mass transmission (tawātur) or by individual reports (āḥād). The first is false, because if its being Qur'an had been established by mass transmission, the necessary knowledge of that would have been achieved, and disagreement about it among the community would have been impossible. The second is also false, because a single report only yields probability (ẓann). If we took it as a path to establishing the Qur'an, the Qur'an would cease to be a certain proof and would become probable. And if that were allowed, it would allow the claim of the Rawāfiḍ that the Qur'an had additions, omissions, alteration and distortion. End of quotation.

This is a sound statement, and the istithnāʾī syllogisms (conditional syllogisms of the form "if not-A then not-B") that he left out of his speech are clear to anyone who is practiced in logic. Its conditional premises need no proof, because they are self-evident from the Law (sharīʿa), so there is no need to spell them out. Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī added in "Aḥkām al-Qur'ān": It is enough for you that the disagreement about it shows it is not Qur'an, since the Qur'an is not subject to disagreement. End of quotation.

ʿAbd al-Wahhāb added: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the Qur'an clear with one uniform clarity, and his manner of clarifying it did not vary in visibility and obscurity so that it would be specific to one or two people. For this reason we are certain that nothing of the Qur'an was left untransmitted to us, and we refuted the claim of the Rawāfiḍ that the Qur'an is a camel-load with the infallible awaited imam. So if the basmala were part of al-Ḥamd (Surat al-Fātiḥa), the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would have clarified it with a clear clarification. End of quotation.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said in "al-ʿĀriḍa": Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr ibn al-Ṭayyib did not speak on jurisprudence except in this particular issue, because it is connected to the foundations (uṣūl).

Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī opposed this argument in "al-Mustaṣfā." He said: The negation that the basmala is part of the Qur'an, if it is established by mass transmission, then it follows that the disagreement would not remain, which is clearly false. If it is established by individual reports, then the Qur'an becomes probable. He said: It cannot be said that the fact that something is not Qur'an is a nonexistence (ʿadam), and nonexistence needs no establishing because it is the original state, unlike the claim that it is Qur'an. Because we reply that although this is a nonexistence, the fact that the basmala is written in the script of the Qur'an weakens the claim that it is not part of the Qur'an. Here we cannot judge that it is not part of the Qur'an except by evidence, and the discussion will come about what that evidence is. Thus it is established that the argument that al-Qāḍī raised binds him. End of quotation.

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī followed him in this in his exegesis. It is not hidden that his argument ended up in circular reasoning (muṣādara), since the basis of the argument of al-Ghazālī and Fakhr al-Dīn became the writing of the basmala in the copies of the Qur'an. We will discuss the verification of that when we speak about the proof of al-Shāfiʿī.

Ibn Rushd, in "Bidāyat al-Mujtahid," criticized the statements of al-Bāqillānī and al-Ghazālī with a discussion that was not well organized, so we will not dwell on it.

As for the second approach, which is argument from transmitted reports, we do not find in the sound Sunna anything that testifies that the basmala is a verse at the beginning of the surahs of the Qur'an. The evidences are six:

The first evidence: What Mālik narrated in the Muwaṭṭaʾ from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Abū Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, exalted is He, said: I have divided the prayer into two halves between Me and My servant, and half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and My servant has what he asks. The servant says: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 2], so I say: My servant has praised Me." And so on. What is meant by "in the prayer" is the recitation in the prayer. The argument from it is that he did not mention "bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm."

The second: The ḥadīth of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb in the Muwaṭṭaʾ and the two Ṣaḥīḥs, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Shall I teach you a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah or the Gospel, before you leave the mosque?" He said: "Yes." When he was about to leave, he said to him: "How do you recite when you begin the prayer?" Ubayy said: "So I recited ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 2] until I came to its end." This is evidence that he did not recite the basmala from it.

The third: What is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Sunan Abī Dāwūd, and Sunan al-Nasāʾī from Anas ibn Mālik, by many chains, that he said: "I prayed behind the Messenger of Allah, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and they used to begin with 'al-Ḥamdu li-Allah Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn,' not mentioning 'bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm,' neither at the beginning of the recitation nor at its end."

The fourth: The ḥadīth of ʿĀʾisha in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and Sunan Abī Dāwūd. She said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to begin the prayer with the takbīr, and the recitation with ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 2].

The fifth: What is in Sunan al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī from ʿAbd Allah ibn Mughaffal, who said: "I prayed with the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān, and I did not hear any of them saying 'bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm.' When you pray, say ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 2]."

[p. 141] The sixth, which is decisive: the practice of the people of Medina. The Prophet's mosque, from the time of the descent of revelation until the time of Mālik, was the place where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the rightly guided caliphs, and the rulers prayed, and behind them prayed the Companions and the scholars. No one was heard reciting "bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm" in the prayers recited aloud. Would any scholar say that part of the surah is recited aloud and part is recited quietly? It has been established by mass transmission that the Prophet and the caliphs did not recite it aloud in the prayers recited aloud. This shows that it is not part of the surah. Had they recited it aloud, people would not have disagreed about it.

There is another evidence that they did not mention here, which is the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾisha about the beginning of revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is considered as a report traced back to the Prophet (marfūʿan). It says: "The angel came to him and said: Read. The Messenger of Allah said: I said: I am not a reader… until he said: Then he squeezed me the third time, then he said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1]." The ḥadīth… He did not say to me "bi-smi Allah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm, read bi-smi rabbika." They mentioned this in the exegesis of Surat al-ʿAlaq and in the explanation of the ḥadīth of the beginning of revelation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 2 of 4):

As for the third approach, which is argumentation from the usage of the Arabic language, the discussion of it proceeds on the basis of taking into account the view of those who hold that the basmala (the formula "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") is a verse of Surat al-Fatiha alone. This requires that two words, namely al-Rahman al-Rahim, be repeated in a speech that is not long and in which there is not a great separation between them, and this is among the things not praised in the domain of balagha (eloquence). This argument was reported by the Imam al-Razi in his tafsir, and he answered it by saying: repetition for the sake of emphasis is frequent in the Qur'an, and affirming that He, exalted is He, is Rahman and Rahim is among the greatest of important matters.

I, for my part, reject his answer, because although repetition has praiseworthy occasions in eloquent speech, such as expressing awe, the context of lamentation, enumeration, or verbal emphasis, the Fatiha has no fitting connection with the purposes of repetition, especially emphasis, since no one denies that He, exalted is He, is Rahman and Rahim. Moreover, the nature of verbal emphasis is that its two words come together without any separation. Therefore it is established that this is a repetition of the word within speech, due to the presence of the requirement to express its meaning by means of the apparent noun rather than the pronoun. Yet this is conditional upon the distance between the two repeated items being such that it removes them from the ear, and you have known that they counted among the eloquence of speech its freedom from excessive repetition; and the closeness between al-Rahman and al-Rahim, when both are repeated, prevents that.

Al-Baydawi answered that the point of the repetition here is to give the reason for deserving praise. Al-Salakuti said: by this he pointed to the refutation of what some Hanafis said: if the basmala were part of al-Fatiha, repetition would necessarily follow. And this answer is not sound, because if the reasoning requires mention of the two attributes al-Rahman al-Rahim, then avoiding repetition requires stripping the basmala
صفحة ١٤٢
which is at the beginning of al-Fatiha of these two attributes, so that al-Fatiha becomes thus: (In the name of God, the praise belongs to God) etc.

As for me, I see in using the path of Arabic taste that it should be based on taking into account the view of those who hold that the basmala is a verse of every surah. From this view there arises that the openings of all the surahs of the Qur'an are alike, and this is not praised in the speech of eloquent writers, since the norm is that variety occurs in openings. Indeed, the scholars of eloquence have counted the most important places of refinement to be the opening and closing of speech, and they mentioned that the openings and closings of surahs come in the best and most complete forms of expression. How then could it be claimed that the openings of its surahs are one single sentence, when most eloquent people, among orators, poets and writers, compete in varying the openings of their compositions, and they criticize whoever adheres to one manner in his speech? So what, then, is your opinion of the most eloquent speech?

As for the argument of the school of al-Shafi'i and those who agree with him, that it is a verse of Surat al-Fatiha, there are many points, which Fakhr al-Din brought to seventeen arguments, of which hardly any stands, after discarding what overlaps, what lies outside the place of dispute, and what has weak or feeble chains, except two matters. The first: numerous hadiths, among them what Abu Hurayra reported, that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The Opening of the Book is seven verses, the first of which is 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.'" And the saying of Umm Salama: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited al-Fatiha and counted "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" and "Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds" [al-Fatiha: 2] as a verse. The second: the consensus that what lies between the two covers is the speech of God.

The answer: as for the hadith of Abu Hurayra, no one from among the men of the Sahih (the authentic collections) has transmitted it; it was only transmitted by al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi, so it falls below the rank of the sahih and does not oppose the sahih hadiths. As for the hadith of Umm Salama, no one from among the men of the Sahih transmitted it except Abu Dawud, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal and al-Bayhaqi transmitted it, and some of its routes were graded sahih. Al-Tahawi criticized it by saying that Ibn Abi Mulayka narrated it, and Ibn Abi Mulayka's hearing from Umm Salama is not established, meaning that it is mursal (with a broken chain). Moreover, he narrated from her something that contradicts it. Furthermore, Shaykh al-Islam Zakariyya stated in his gloss on the tafsir of al-Baydawi that it was not transmitted with the wording mentioned, but was transmitted with wordings that indicate that "In the name of God" is a verse on its own, so it cannot be taken from it that it is part of al-Fatiha. Furthermore, this leads to establishing Qur'anicity by means other than mass transmission, which the Muslims reject.

As for the consensus that what lies between the two covers is the speech of God, the answer is that it only requires that the basmala is Qur'an, and this is not disputed. As for whether the places where it was written in the Mushaf are among those that must be recited therein,
صفحة ١٤٣
that is a matter that follows the transmission of the readers and the reports of the authentic Sunna, and so it returns to the preceding evidences.

All of this is based on granting that the Companions did not write the names of the surahs, nor whether they are Meccan or Medinan, in the Mushaf, and that this was the work of later generations; this is the explicit statement of 'Abd al-Hakim in his gloss on al-Baydawi. But if it is established that some of the early generation wrote these, as is the apparent meaning of the words of the exegetes, the usulis and the readers, as in Lata'if al-Isharat by al-Qastallani, and as is implied by the later generations' writing of these, because they would not dare to add to what the early generation did, then argument from the writing is then null from its root. And the claim that the names of the surahs were written in an ink of a color different from the ink of the Qur'an is refuted by the fact that what is observed in the Mushafs of the early generation is that their ink is of one color, and colouring was not widespread.

Some have argued with what al-Bukhari reported "from Anas, that he was asked how the recitation of the Prophet was, and he said: it was elongated, then he recited: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, elongating 'In the name of God,' and elongating 'al-Rahman,' and elongating 'al-Rahim'" — end of quote. There is no proof in this, because the pronoun in "recited" and the pronoun in "elongating" both refer to Anas, and he only brought the basmala as an illustration of the manner of recitation because the basmala is well known.

The argument of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak and the second of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i is what Muslim reported from Anas, who said: "While the Messenger of God was among us one day, he dozed off briefly, then raised his head smiling. We said: What made you laugh, O Messenger of God? He said: A surah was just revealed to me, and he recited: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. (Surely We have given you al-Kawthar [al-Kawthar: 1]) the surah." They said: and because of the consensus that what lies between the two covers is the speech of God, and because the Companions affirmed it in the Mushafs while being keen not to introduce into the Qur'an what is not part of it, and for this reason they did not write "Amin" in al-Fatiha. The answer to the hadith is that we deny that he recited the basmala as being part of the surah; rather he began with it when intending to recite, because it suffices instead of the seeking of refuge when the one who says the basmala intends the estimate "I seek refuge in the name of God" and omits the object of the verb. And it is necessary to interpret it as such, because its narrator Anas ibn Malik affirmed in his other hadith that he did not hear the Messenger of God say the basmala in prayer.

If they refuse to interpret it in the way we have interpreted it, then Anas's report is inconsistent in a way that requires its discarding.

The clear truth regarding the basmala at the beginnings of surahs is that it was written to separate between surahs, so that the separation would be fitting to the beginning of the Mushaf, and so that it would not be a formula from outside the Qur'an. Abu Dawud reported in his Sunan, and al-Tirmidhi graded it sahih,
صفحة ١٤٤
from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: I said to 'Uthman ibn 'Affan: What made you proceed to (Surat) Bara'a, which is of the mi'in (surahs of about a hundred verses), and to al-Anfal, which is of the mathani (oft-repeated), and place them among the seven long ones, and not write between them a line of "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"? 'Uthman said: The Prophet, when verses were revealed to him, would call some of those who wrote for him and say to him: place this verse in the surah in which such and such is mentioned; or a verse or two would be revealed to him and he would say the like. Al-Anfal was among the first things revealed to him at Medina, and Bara'a was among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, and its story resembled its story, and the Messenger of God was taken [in death] without explaining to us that it was part of it, so I assumed it was part of it. From here I placed it among the seven long ones and did not write between them a line of "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."

I see in this a clear indication that the basmala was not written between surahs except for al-Anfal and Bara'a, and only when the Qur'an was collected into one Mushaf in the time of 'Uthman; and that it was not written at the beginnings of surahs in the sheets that Zayd ibn Thabit collected in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, since each surah then had a separate sheet, as was mentioned in the eighth introduction among the introductions to this tafsir.

Furthermore, the basmala is disputed as to whether it is a verse at the beginning of every surah other than Bara'a, or a verse at the beginning of al-Fatiha alone, or not a verse at the beginning of any of the surahs. The readers agreed on reciting the basmala when beginning the recitation of a surah from its start, other than Bara'a, and they transmitted this from those from whom they received. As for those among them who transmit, by ijtihad or taqlid, that the basmala is a verse at the beginning of every surah other than Bara'a, their position is clear, and reciting the basmala at the beginnings of surahs is obligatory for them without doubt, in prayer and otherwise. As for those who do not transmit the basmala as a verse at the beginning of all surahs, or of all except al-Fatiha, their recitation of the basmala at the beginning of a surah when starting a surah not preceded by the recitation of another surah is justified by seeking blessing (tayammun) by following the practice of the scribes of the Mushaf, that is, intending imitation in merely the beginning of an act, likening the beginning of recitation to the beginning of writing. Thus their recitation of the basmala is a recommended matter, in imitation of the Companions who wrote the Mushaf in recitation. Accordingly, for these, reciting the basmala is like uttering the seeking of refuge, and like the tahlil and takbir between some surahs at the end of the mufassal. They do not recite the basmala in obligatory prayer; and when these people recite in obligatory prayer, their recitation follows what their understanding has reached regarding the basmala, whether by ijtihad or taqlid.

By this you know that one should not take from their recitation a statement by them that the basmala is a verse
صفحة ١٤٥
from the beginning of every surah, as did the author of al-Kashshaf and al-Baydawi.

They differed concerning reciting the basmala when not beginning a surah from its start, that is, reciting the basmala between two surahs.

Warsh from Nafi' in the most famous of his transmissions, and Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, Ya'qub and Khalaf do not recite the basmala between two surahs. This is explained by the fact that imitation of the scribes of the Mushaf is specific to the beginning, and by their interpreting the writing of the basmala in the Mushaf as a sign of the beginning of a surah, not as a separator; for had the basmala been a sign of separation between a surah and the one following it, it would not have been written at the beginning of al-Fatiha. Their practice was therefore sound, since they combined what they transmitted from their predecessors with the evidence of the intention of seeking blessing; and the evidence for their opinion is that the basmala is not a verse from the beginning of every surah.

Qalun from Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far recite the basmala between two surahs except between al-Anfal and Bara'a, and they counted it among the Sunna of recitation. Their share in this is nothing but following their predecessors, since not all of them were among the people of ijtihad; and perhaps they extended the intention of seeking blessing by likeness to the scribes of the Mushaf, in signaling the beginning of a surah and signaling the ending of the one before it.

The Muslims agreed to omit the basmalah (the formula "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful") at the beginning of Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). The reason for this has already been explained above. The imams gave other reasons for it as well, which apply at the beginning of Surah Bara'ah. Al-Jahiz mentions in al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin that Mu'arrij al-Sadusi al-Basri heard a man say, "The Commander of the Faithful returns [a reply] to the wronged," so Mu'arrij went back to his copy of the Qur'an and added "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" in front of Bara'ah. What Mu'arrij did, if it is authentically transmitted from him, is to be understood as a jest and a joke, not as a serious act.

This shows that the differences among the readers (qurra') regarding the recitation of the basmalah at the beginnings of surahs and in connection with the surah, at various places in the Qur'an, as was mentioned earlier, have no bearing on the disagreement over the ruling on reciting it in prayer. Its recitation in prayer is governed by careful examination of the evidences, and the positions of the readers are not counted among the sources of jurisprudence (fiqh). Their readings are transmitted narrations and a practice followed in reciting the Qur'an, without reference to the rules governing the transmission of Qur'anic readings, whether mutawatir (widely transmitted) or otherwise, and without reference to obligation, recommendation, or option. The reader recites as he was taught by his teachers,

[Page 146]

and does not consider whether what he recites must be recited exactly as he recited it or whether that is not required. Their practices in prayer follow their inclinations in jurisprudence, whether through ijtihad (independent reasoning) or taqlid (imitation). This also clarifies the error of those who thought that the disagreement of the jurists over affirming or denying the basmalah is based on the disagreement of the readers, and it clarifies the laxity of the author of al-Kashshaf in listing the positions of the readers in the same sequence as the positions of the jurists.

The mujtahids disagreed only because of the evidences explained earlier. As for their general agreement with the readers of their own regions on this question, its cause is the spread, among the people of that age, of the view held by their jurists on these issues, or the spread of the evidences that the mujtahids received from their own teachers among the people of that age, even before the mujtahid emerged. An example is the precedence of Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym in not reciting the basmalah before Malik adopted the view that it is not part of the surah. This is because Malik received the evidences for denying that it is part of the surah from the scholars of Madina, and from them or from their teachers, just as Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym received them.

Since we have adopted the school of Malik and are satisfied with his sources in holding that the basmalah is not a verse at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara, it is incumbent upon us not to address its interpretation here, and to postpone it to the discussion of God's words in Surat al-Naml: ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"﴾ [al-Naml: 30]. However, since we found that all of our predecessors among the exegetes (mufassirun) did not neglect the discussion of the basmalah at this point, we followed their example, since this has become the terminology of the exegetes.

Know that the complement of the prepositional phrase in "bismi Allah" is omitted, and its estimated form here is "aqra'" (I recite). The reason for omitting the complement of the prepositional phrase is that the basmalah was prescribed at the start of good deeds, so its complement was omitted in an obligatory manner for brevity, relying on the context. The Qur'an reports the words of Pharaoh's magicians when they began their magic: ﴿So they cast their ropes and their staves, and said: "By the might of Pharaoh"﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf mentions that the people of the pre-Islamic period used to say at the beginning of their actions: "In the name of al-Lat, in the name of al-Uzza." Thus the prepositional phrase is an adverbial complement (zarf laghw) governed by the omitted verb and attached to it, and it is not a fixed adverbial (zarf mustaqarr) such as those that occur as predicates. The indication of the complement is conveyed by the action that was begun. Therefore it must be a specific verb of the kind that signifies the meaning of the action undertaken, rather than a general complement, such as "abtadi'" (I begin), because the context indicating the complement is the verb undertaken and begun with the basmalah. Thus the estimated element must be the word that signifies that verb. This does not apply to the disagreement among the grammarians about whether the complement of adverbial phrases should be estimated as a noun, such as "ka'in" (existing) or "mustaqirr" (fixed), or as a verb, such as "kana" (was) or "istaqarra" (settled). That disagreement concerns adverbial phrases that occur as predicates or circumstantial expressions (hal), and it is based on a conflict between the requirement of estimating a noun, which is that it is the basic form for predicates and circumstantial expressions, and the requirement of estimating a verb, which is that it is the basic form for action, since what is here is an adverbial complement (zarf laghw), and the basic rule for it is that it transmits action from verbs and is attached to them. Also, the aim of one who begins with the basmalah is that all of his action be accompanied by the blessing of God's name. Therefore it is appropriate to estimate the complement of the preposition as a word indicating the action begun, and this is more suitable for generalizing the blessing to all parts of the action. Beginning [with a noun] is less general in this respect. Thus estimating a general verb makes it specific, and estimating a specific verb makes it general. This resembles a riddle.

This estimate is one of the estimated elements indicated by context, like the words of the one who calls to the groom: "With joy and children," and the words of the traveler upon arrival and departure: "In the name of God and blessings," and the words of Arab women when they escort the bride: "With good fortune and blessing, and upon the auspicious bird." Therefore, estimating the verb here is clear. This omission is supported by a benefit: the basmalah is suitable for every doer beginning an action, so he does not need to deviate from the wording of the Qur'an when quoting it. The omission here is of the kind called brevity (ijaz), because it omits what may be stated explicitly in speech. This differs from the complements of fixed adverbial phrases, such as "'indaka khayr" (there is good with you), since people do not state the complement in such cases, so they do not say "khayr ka'in 'indaka" (good existing with you). For this reason, they considered such a phrase as in his words: ﴿Indeed you are like the night, which is overtaking me﴾ to be equality (musawat) rather than brevity, despite the omission of the complement in it. Since the complement is omitted, it must be estimated in its position, preceding the word it governs, as is the basic form of the sentence, since there is no intention here for the basmalah to convey exclusivity (hasr). The claim of the author of al-Kashshaf that it is estimated as postponed is excessive and unacceptable, especially in the case of omission. So the more suitable approach is to estimate it according to the basic form.

The "ba'" is the ba' of accompaniment (mulabasa), which means association, and it is also the ba' of attachment (ilsaq). These are synonyms in indicating this meaning, as in God's words: ﴿grows with oil﴾ and in the expression "with joy and children." This meaning is the most common and best known of the meanings of ba'. Sibawayh said: "Attachment never leaves the ba', and all its varied meanings return to it." Therefore the author of al-Kashshaf said: "This aspect, namely accompaniment, is more eloquent and better," that is, better than making the ba' indicate the instrument, that is, more fitting in Arabic and better, because it adds more blessing through the association of all parts of the action with God's name.

The "ism" (name) is a word made to indicate a sensible or abstract entity, by its individual or by its type. The imams of Basra derived it from "sumuww," which means elevation, because elevation is realized in the uses of the word "ism," even by figurative interpretation. The basic meaning of "ism" in the speech of the Arabs is "'alam" (designation), since proper names are only given to something of importance. This is taking account of the basic and usual case; otherwise proper names may be given to things not of importance, as they said "fujjar" (wicked ones) is the proper name for the wicked. According to the Basrans, its basic form is from the defective root with waw, so it is either "simw" on the pattern of "himl," or "sumw" on the pattern of "qufl." The final radical was deleted purely for lightness, or because of frequent use. For this reason, the case endings (i'rab) apply to the remaining letter. If its final radical had been deleted for a morphological reason, the case ending would have been estimated on the deleted letter, as in "qadin" (judge) and "jawari" (girls). When the case endings applied to the remaining letter, which was quiescent, they transferred its quiescence to the moving letter, which is the first letter of the word, and they introduced a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) to allow pronunciation with a quiescent letter, since the Arabs do not favor beginning with a quiescent letter, their language being based on lightness. They allowed the introduction of the hamza as a second stage of lightening, which is returning the word to a triliteral form, because nouns that remain with two letters after deletion, such as "yad" (hand) and "dam" (blood), are not free of heaviness. This is evidence that the hamza was not introduced to compensate for the deleted letter, since otherwise they would have introduced it in "yad," "dam," and "ghad" (tomorrow).

They argued that its original form is as stated by citing its plural on the pattern of "af'al," in which a hamza appears at the end, which is changed from a final waw following the alif of the plural. They also argued that it is plural on "asami," which is the plural of the plural on the pattern of "afa'il," with the plural yā' merged into the final radical, and it may be lightened as in "athafi" and "amani." They also argued that it is diminutive on "sumayy." And that its verb is "sammaytu," and these are clear proofs that its origin is the defective root with waw. And they argued that it is said "suma" like "huda," because they formed it on the pattern "fi'l" like "ratub," so the moving waw changes to alif after a fatha, and they cited on this the verse of Abu Khalid al-Qanani, the reciter (rajiz):

"God named you a blessed name, and gave you a preference above others."

Ibn Ya'ish said: "There is no proof in it, because it is possible that it is a dialect of one who says 'sum,' and the accusative in it is an accusative of case ending, not an accusative of morphological alteration." 'Abd al-Hakim refuted this, saying that its writing with imala (vocalic inclination) indicates otherwise. In my view, writing is not a matter on which transmission depends, so perhaps those who wrote it with yā' were those who thought it was defective (maqsur). Moreover, its analogical writing is with alif in all cases, since it is from waw, except when one wants to avoid confusing it with the accusative alif. The view of the Basrans is more probable from the standpoint of the morphological forms of this word.

The Kufans held that its original form is "wisم" with a kasra on the waw, because it derives from "simah," which means mark. The waw was deleted and replaced by the hamzat al-wasl, to keep it at three letters, and then this was used to lighten it in connection. It seems they thought there was no basis for deriving it from "sumuww," since it is used for things that are not elevated. You know the answer to this. The view of the Kufans is more probable from the standpoint of derivation, but not morphology. Moreover, the hamzat al-wasl is not known to occur on something whose beginning has been deleted. They rejected the Basran argument from its morphological forms by saying that these forms may come from metathesis (qalb makani), so that the original form was "ism" from "wasm," then the waw, which is the first radical, was moved to the final position, so that it could be deleted. They replied that this is far-fetched because it departs from the basic form, and that metathesis does not apply to the word in all its forms, otherwise the original root of that word would not be known.

Scholars of the language agree that *al-tasarif* (morphological derivation, *sarf*) is the means by which one recognizes what is an augmented letter and what is original, and what has been altered from something else. Ibn Hazm, in *Kitab al-Milal wa al-Nihal*, claimed that both positions of the Basrans and the Kufans are corrupt, invented by the grammarians, and not transmitted from the Arabs. He also held that the word *ism* (name) is not derived but is a fixed noun. He pursued this with insults against them, and it is a remarkable audacity. God the Exalted has said: ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43].

The word *ism* is inserted as a genitive construct before the Name of God when one says *bismillah* ("in the name of God"), and not *billah* ("by God"). The intended meaning is that the act undertaken be one of the affairs of the people of monotheism, who are marked by the name of the One God. For this reason the word *ism* is inserted in every context that has this purpose, such as naming God over a sacrifice. God has said: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am: 118], and: ﴿And what is it with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned?﴾ [al-An'am: 119]. It is likewise used with acts intended for blessing, auspiciousness and help, such as: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1]. Thus the *ism* of God is what can be joined to acts, not His essence. In such a context it is not appropriate to say *billah*, because then the meaning would be that one seeks from God facility and a disposition of His power, and that is not the intended purpose of beginning the act. God's saying ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 74] is a command to say "Glory be to God," and His saying "and glorify Him" is a command to declare His essence and attributes free of deficiencies. So the use of the word *ism* in this sense is like the use of camel brands among the tribes, like the tribes' emblem by which they recognize one another, and like the armies' agreed-upon battle-cry.

In summary, every context in which the aim is blessing and affiliation with the One Lord, the Necessarily Existent, has the verb transferred to the word *ism* of God, as in His saying: ﴿And he said, "Board it; in the name of God is its course and its anchoring"﴾ [Hud: 41]. In the hadith of the supplication upon lying down: "In Your name, my Lord, I lay down my side, and in Your name I raise it." Likewise, in a context where the mention of the name of God the Exalted is intended, as in His saying ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 74], meaning: say "Glory be to God," as in "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" [al-A'la: 1]. And in every context where seeking facility and help from God the Exalted is intended, the verb requested is transferred to the proper name of the Essence, in respect of His attributes of creation and origination, as in His saying: ﴿So prostrate to Him﴾, and in the hadith: "O God, by You we enter the morning and by You we enter the evening," meaning by Your power and Your will. Likewise, in a context where the direction of the verb toward God the Exalted is intended, as in His saying: ﴿So prostrate to Him and glorify Him﴾ [al-Insan: 26], meaning: declare His essence and reality free of deficiencies. Thus the meaning of *bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim* is: "I read, with a reading joined to the blessing of this blessed Name."

It has also been reported that the Arabs used the word *ism* in broader ways. Sometimes they mean by it what is synonymous with the named thing, as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"I was informed by Zur'ah, and foolishness is as its name,
it brings me strange poems."

He means that foolishness is itself, and is not made known to people by more than its name. This is close to the use of the demonstrative in His saying: ﴿And thus We made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning: like that clear and well-known making. And they use the word *ism* as an empty, superfluous insertion, as in the verse of Labid: "Until the year's end, then the *ism* of peace upon you both," meaning: then peace upon you both. This is not specific to the word *ism*; it occurs with its synonyms, such as *kalimah* (word) in His saying: ﴿And He made binding upon them the word of piety﴾ [al-Fath: 26]. Likewise the word *lafz* (utterance) appears in the verse of Bashshar, satirizing:

"Thus your father was preferred for his generosity,
and remained in the utterance of generosity, repeating."

The name, or what has its meaning, is sometimes used as a metonym for the existence of the named thing. Among this is God's saying: ﴿And they have set up with God partners. Say: "Name them."﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]. The command here is one of challenge, meaning: prove their existence and assign them names. These are other uses, and the mention of the name of God in the *basmalah* is not of this kind. I have mentioned them only because some exegetes mixed them into the explanation of the *basmalah*. I have recorded them here for clarification, so that your consideration of them may be broad. Hold firmly to them, and do not follow scattered paths.

Some have spoken about the feature of elongating the letter *ba'* in the writing of the *basmalah* with words that are all unconvincing. What appears to me is that when the Companions compiled the Mushaf, they elongated it in Surat al-Naml to indicate that it is the beginning of the book of Solomon, and so it is part of what is reported. When they made it a marker for the openings of the surahs, they transmitted it in its written form. The elongation of the *ba'* in it is suitable to be adopted as a model for beginning a new purpose in speech with a thick or colored letter.

The discussion of the name of God (*ism al-Jalalah*) and its attributes comes with the explanation of His saying ﴿All praise is for God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2], ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Fatihah: 3].

As for the appropriateness of combining the proper name of God with the two attributes *al-Rahman al-Rahim* in the *basmalah*, al-Baydawi said: when the one who names intends to seek help from the worshipped Truth, described as the bestower of all blessings, great and small, he mentions the proper name of the Essence, as an indication that He deserves to be sought for help by His very Essence. Then he mentions the attribute *al-Rahman*, indicating that help in righteous deeds, which are blessings, comes from Him. The mention of *al-Rahim* is for reasons that we will mention when discussing the conjunction of the attribute *al-Rahim* to the attribute *al-Rahman*.

Imam Muhammad 'Abduh said: the Christians used to begin their supplications and the like with "in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit," indicating the three hypostases in their belief. So the opening of the Book of Islam came as a refutation of them, alerting them that the One God, even if His names are many, is only a multiplicity of attributes and not a multiplicity of named beings. He means that it is a refutation of them through exposing their error and dullness. If it is correct that the Christians' openings and supplications included this, since the transmitter is trustworthy, then this is a subtle point.

In my view, the *basmalah*, or what is synonymous with it, was already current on the tongues of the prophets from the time of Abraham, peace be upon him. It is therefore part of the speech of the Hanifiyyah. God related that Abraham said to his father: ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you﴾ [Maryam: 45], and said: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He is ever gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47]. The meaning of *hafiy* (gracious) is close to the meaning of *rahim* (merciful). And He related his saying: ﴿And accept our repentance; indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]. The mention of its synonym appears in the letter of Solomon to the Queen of Sheba: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Naml: 30], ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml: 31]. It is presumed that Solomon, in opening his letter with the *basmalah*, followed an inherited practice from the time of Abraham, which Abraham made an enduring word among the heirs of his prophethood. God revived this practice in Islam among what He revealed of the Hanifiyyah, as He said: ﴿The religion of your father Abraham. He named you "the Muslims" before this﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

[p. 150]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 1, verse 2 (part 1 of 4):

[152]
﴿Al-hamdu lillah﴾ [All praise is due to Allah]

The matter, when addressing someone with an important command that the addressee has not encountered in a discourse of its kind before, requires that he first be made comfortable before the intended matter is delivered, that he be prepared to receive it, that he be made eager to hear it, and that his soul be trained to care about acting upon it, so that he is ready to receive it by clearing himself of everything that could hinder him from benefiting from guidance, such as obstinacy and stubbornness, or a mind filled with misguided illusions. For the soul hardly benefits from admonitions and warnings, and wisdom and sound reasoning do not shine within it as long as obstinacy and slander cling to it and the whisperings of Satan corrupt its right judgment. When Allah willed that this surah be the first of the surahs of the Glorious Book, by the directive of the Prophet (ﷺ) as has been mentioned just above, Allah, exalted is He, alerted the readers of His Book and the openers of its codex to the foundations of this inner purification, by teaching them to begin with the intimate prayer contained in Surat al-Fatihah from His saying ﴿Iyyaka na'budu﴾ [You alone we worship] to the end of the surah. For it contains great foundations:

The first: clearing oneself of negation (ta'til) and polytheism (shirk), by what is contained in ﴿Iyyaka na'budu﴾.
The second: clearing oneself of thoughts of self-sufficiency from Him, by disowning power and strength before His greatness, by what is contained in ﴿wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾ [and You alone we ask for help].
The third: the desire to adorn oneself with right judgment and seeking guidance, by what is contained in ﴿ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim﴾ [guide us to the straight path].
The fourth: the desire to adorn oneself with the good example, by what is contained in ﴿sirat alladhina an'amta 'alayhim﴾ [the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour].
The fifth: resolve for safety from manifest error, by what is contained in ﴿ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim﴾ [not of those who have incurred wrath].
The sixth: resolve for the safety of their thinking from being mixed with the doubts of falsehood disguised in the form of truth, which is what is called error (dalal), because dalal is deviation from the intended path, by what is contained in ﴿wa la al-dallin﴾ [nor of those who are astray].

If you survey the principles of success for the guide in his guiding and for the seeker of guidance in his receiving, with all their multiplicity and branches, you will find them centred around these six pillars, so be discerning in tracing them out. Perhaps I will expand upon their details shortly.

He who taught the people of the Qur'an what it contains of the essence of the paths of right guidance, in a manner that no one but the Knower of the unseen can encompass, did not neglect to guide them to adorn themselves with the beauty of virtues, which is to value blessing as it deserves by thanking its Giver. So He showed them how to crown their intimate prayer with praise of the Bestower of intellect and the Giver of success. Therefore the opening of every important discourse with praise has been the custom of the Glorious Book.

[153]
Thus, Surat al-Fatihah, with what has been established, is sent down from the Qur'an in the position of the preface (dibaja) to the book, or the introduction to the sermon. This method has a great standing in the craft of Arabic composition, and it is more helpful to understanding and more conducive to awareness.

Al-Fatihah has laid down for composers three rules for the introduction:

The first rule: brevity of the introduction, lest the souls of listeners grow weary through the long wait for the intended matter, and this is evident in al-Fatihah. It also serves as a model for orators, so that they do not lengthen the introduction, lest they be attributed with incapacity (ayy), for the longer the introduction, the less the purpose is served. From this appears the wisdom of placing it before the long surahs, although it is a short surah.

The second: that it point to the intended purpose, which is what is called baraat al-istihlal (the skill of the opening), because that prepares the listeners to hear the detail of what will come to them, so they make ready to receive it if they are among those who receive, or to criticise and complete it if they are at that level. It also indicates the orator's mastery of the purpose and his confidence in the soundness of his view of it, to the extent that he alerts the listeners to his awareness. In this there is a model for orators, so that they encompass the aims of their speech. The inclusion of this in al-Fatihah has already been explained when discussing the reason it is named Umm al-Qur'an.

The third: that the introduction be among the comprehensive words (jawami' al-kalim), and the scholars of rhetoric have clarified this when they mentioned the places where the speaker should take care to refine his expression.

The fourth: that it begin with the praise of Allah. The Qur'an was sent down as guidance for mankind and as an explanation of the rulings by which the people's affairs are set right in their immediate and ultimate lives, in their livelihood and their return. And since the souls of the community were not accustomed to this, it was necessary that those addressed by it be prepared to receive it, and their preparation is recognised by their showing the readiness of souls by clearing themselves of everything that could prevent benefiting from these beneficial teachings, namely by stripping their souls of obstinacy and stubbornness, and of mixing their knowledge with grave errors. So there is no escape for them, before receiving that wisdom and reflection, from being marked with the mark of virtue and being cleansed of base vileness.

Al-Fatihah thus contains an intimate prayer to the Creator that encompasses exemption from negation (ta'til), atheism and naturalism (dahriyya) by what is contained in His saying ﴿Malik yawm al-din﴾ [Master of the Day of Judgment] (Fatihah 4), and from associating partners by what is contained in ﴿Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾, and from stubbornness and obstinacy by what is contained in ﴿ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim sirat alladhina an'amta 'alayhim﴾. For the request for guidance is an acknowledgment of the need for knowledge, and describing the path as straight is an acknowledgment that among knowledge there is what is true and there is what is mixed with doubts and error. Whoever acknowledges these two matters has prepared himself to follow the better of them. And it is also from freedom from the errors that afflict sound sciences and true laws, so that they take away their benefit,

[154]
and lower their possessor to a level lower than where the simple ignorant person stands. This is by what is contained in His saying (﴿ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa la al-dallin﴾), as we have summarised shortly. For this reason this surah was named Umm al-Qur'an, as has been mentioned.

When the believers were taught this wondrous intimate prayer, which no one but the Knower of the unseen, glory be to Him, can encompass in His speech, He placed praise before it, so that those who engage in intimate prayer would likewise place it at the start of their supplication, following the manner of the eloquent Arabs when addressing the great, to open their address and their request with praise and good remembrance.

Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said, praising Abd Allah ibn Jud'an:

Shall I mention my need, or has your modesty sufficed me? Indeed your disposition is modesty.
When a man praises you one day, his praise suffices him from having to ask.

Thus the opening of speech with praise, the custom of the Glorious Book, became for every eloquent and accomplished person. From that day onward the Muslims have named every precious speech that does not begin with praise "abtar" (cut off), relying on the hadith of Abu Hurayra from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every matter of importance that is not begun with the praise of Allah, or with praise, is cut off (aqta')." The sermon of Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan which he delivered in Basra was named "al-batra'" (the truncated), because he did not begin it with praise.

Surat al-Fatihah was therefore sent down from the Qur'an in the position of the preface to the book, or the introduction to the sermon.

This has an important standing in the craft of composition, for placing an introduction before the intended purpose is more helpful to understanding and more conducive to grasping it.

Praise (hamd) is the commendation of the beautiful, that is, the description of the beautiful that is voluntary (ikhtiyari), whether it is an act such as generosity and relieving the distressed, or other than that, such as courage. They have made commendation (thana') a genus for praise (hamd), so it is more general than it and is not its opposite.

Thana' is mention with good in an absolute sense. Whoever said that thana' is used for mention in an absolute sense, even with evil, is an anomaly, and they attributed this to Ibn al-Qatta'; what deceived him in this was what occurs in the hadith, his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever you commend with good, Paradise is due to him, and whoever you commend with evil, the Fire is due to him." This is only a metaphor, prompted by verbal correspondence (mushakala lafziyya), and an allusion that whoever speaks about a Muslim should speak with praise or else remain silent; so he called their mention of evil "thana'," as an alert to this. As for what is used for good and evil alike, it is nithaa' with the nun pronounced first, and it is more frequent in evil, as has been said. As for madh (praise), it has been disputed: the majority hold that madh is more general than hamd, for it may be upon voluntary description and other than it.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Hamd and madh are brothers (akhawan)." It was said he meant "brothers" in the great derivation (ishtiqaq kabir), like jabadha and jadhaba; and that this is a technical usage of his in al-Kashshaf regarding the sense of the brotherhood of the two words, lest the apparent sense of his speech imply that madh is applied to praise of voluntary beauty. But this understanding is not correct, and what the verifying commentators of al-Kashshaf hold is that by "brothers" here he meant synonymy, since this is the apparent sense of his words; and because he explicitly said in al-Fa'iq, "hamd is madh and description with beauty"; and because he mentioned dhamm (blame) as the opposite of hamd, when he said in al-Kashshaf, "and its opposite is dhamm," although it is widely known that dhamm is the opposite of madh. The custom of the scholars of language is to mean by "opposite" the counterpart, not what is equal to the opposite, so that it could be answered that he meant by the opposite what does not combine with the meaning, and dhamm does not combine with hamd, even if its meaning is not the lifting of the meaning of hamd but the lifting of the meaning of madh; yet negating the more general, which is madh, entails negating the more specific, which is hamd, because this is not what the scholars of language intend, that is, even if such a thing is tolerated in Arab usage, as in the saying of Zuhayr:

"Whoever places kindness in other than its people, his praise will become blame upon him, and he will regret."

For the speech of scholars is built on precision and exactness.

Then it was disputed what Sahib al-Kashshaf intended by their synonymy: whether they are synonymous in being restricted to praise of voluntary beauty, or synonymous in not being restricted to the voluntary. On the first reading, al-Sayyid al-Sharif adopted it, and it is the apparent sense of Sa'd al-Din's words; al-Sayyid argued that he stated this explicitly in his commentary on the saying of the Exalted, ﴿But Allah has endeared to you faith﴾ (al-Hujurat 7), when he said: "If you say, the Arabs praise beauty and comeliness of faces, which is praise accepted among people, I say: what justified that is that they saw that fine appearance and pleasing aspect generally indicate a satisfactory inner reality and praiseworthy characteristics. Moreover, among the verifying authorities and scholars of meanings are those who rejected the soundness of that and considered the one praising with it mistaken, and restricted praise to describing the mothers of virtues, such as eloquence, courage, justice, chastity, and what branches from them." End.

On the second reading, that he intended by synonymy the removal of the condition of voluntariness from both, the verifying scholar 'Abd al-Hakim al-Sialkuti adopted it in his glosses on the tafsir, as an assumption or transmission rather than a preference, on the basis that this is the apparent sense of his words in al-Kashshaf and al-Fa'iq, since he removed the condition of voluntariness in explaining madh as commendation of beauty, and made them synonymous despite that.

Thus the difficulty is removed from our praising God, Exalted is He, for His essential attributes such as knowledge and power, but not for attributes of action; though the removal of the difficulty is also evident according to the preference of the majority. For what was directed at them, that their doctrine entails that God, Exalted is He, should not be praised for His attributes because they are essential, and so they are not described as chosen, since choice entails the possibility of being qualified, has been answered by them in one of three ways: either that those sublime attributes are treated as if they were chosen, because their possessor is independent; or that the ordering of chosen effects upon them makes them like the chosen ones; or that what is meant by "chosen" is that the one praised acts by choice, even if what is praised is not chosen. In my view, the answer is that we say: the condition of "chosen" in the reality of praise, according to its affirmer, is to exclude attributes that are not chosen, because what is not chosen in us is not among the attributes of perfection, since the effects that necessitate praise do not follow from it. So the condition of choice in our praise is an addition to the realization of the perfection of the one praised. As for the absence of choice that is specific to the divine essential attributes, it is not an expression of deficiency in His attributes; rather it is a perfection arising from the necessity of the attribute for the essence, given the eternity of the attribute. Thus the absence of choice in the attributes of God, Exalted is He, is an addition to perfection, because the like of those attributes in us are not necessary to the essence and not constantly attached to it. So the absence of choice in the attributes of God, Exalted is He, is evidence of increased perfection, while in us it is evidence of deficiency. Whatever is a deficiency in us, in one respect, may be a perfection for God, Exalted is He, in another respect, like the absence of offspring. Therefore there is no need for the answers based on "descent" (tanzil), whether by reference to the attribute or by reference to the qualified. Moreover, directing praise to God, Exalted is He, with the root ḥ-m-d is the furthest that the language, established for conveying the meanings current among its people, can be stretched to express. So when perceptions relating to lofty realities came upon them, He expressed to them those realities by the nearest thing to their speech.

"Al-ḥamdu" is in the nominative by the inchoative (mubtada') in all the transmitted readings, and "lillāhi" is its predicate (khabar). The lām in "lillāhi" is connected to the general stable/existential sense (al-kawn wal-istiqrar al-'amm), like the rest of the prepositional phrases used as predicates. Here it is among the verbal nouns (maṣādir) that came in place of their verbs with the sense of informing; its original form is the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq), as if replaced from its verb, and the sense of the sentence is "naḥmadu ḥamdan lillāh" (we praise, praise to God). Therefore they are obliged to omit their verbs along with them.

Sibawayh said: "This is the chapter of the verbal nouns that are put in the accusative by implying an unused verb, such as your saying: saqyan (watering), ra'yan (pasturing), khay'atan (ruin), bu's (misery), and al-ḥadhara (beware), in place of ihdhar, so it needs no complement. As for their saying saqyan laka, like

"saqyan wa ra'yan li-dhāka al-'ātibi al-zārī"

it is only so that they may clarify the meaning by way of supplication." Then he said after several chapters: "This is the chapter of what is put in the accusative by implying a verb omitted from being expressed, from the verbal nouns outside supplication. Of this is your saying: ḥamdan [page 157] wa shukran, not kufran wa 'ajaban. This is put in the accusative by implying the verb, as if you said: 'aḥmadu Allāha ḥamdan.' The verb is omitted here because they made this a substitute for the utterance of the verb, as they did in the chapter of supplication. Some of this has also come in the nominative, which is begun and then predicated upon, i.e., something is said about it."

Then he said after another chapter: "This is a chapter in which the verbal nouns are preferred to be inchoative, with what follows them predicated upon them, such as your saying: al-ḥamdu lillāh, al-'ajabu laka, al-waylu lahu. They preferred the nominative in it because it became definite, and it is a predicate, i.e., not a performative utterance; so it was strong at the beginning, i.e., since it was a statement and not a supplication, and was definite by the article, the conditions for the inchoative were met in it, because its being in the sense of informing prepares the side of meaning for being a statement, and its being definite makes it correct to be an inchoative, like 'Abdullāh, al-rajul, and al-ladhī, which you know among definites, because the inchoative is in fact a statement, and the best arrangement, when a definite and an indefinite are combined, is to begin with the well-known, which is the basic order of speech. Not every word-structure is made in this way, just as not every word of these verbal nouns takes the article; so if you said al-saqya laka and al-ra'ya laka it would not be permitted, meaning it is restricted to what is heard."

Know that "al-ḥamdu lillāh," though you begin it, contains the sense of the accusative, being a substitute for the utterance "aḥmadu Allāh."

We have heard many Arabs say: "al-turāba laka and al-'ajaba laka." The explanation of its accusative is like its explanation when it is indefinite, as if you said: "ḥamdan wa 'ajaban," then you brought "laka" to make clear whom you mean, and you did not make it a predicate upon which you begin. End of Sibawayh's words, abridged. We have cited it here because it is the most eloquent statement on the varieties of this verbal noun in Arabic usage and its employment. It is what the author of al-Kashshaf alluded to with his words: "Its original form is the accusative, by implying its verb, as it is one of the verbal nouns which the Arabs put in the accusative with implied verbs in the sense of informing, like their saying shukran, kufran, 'ajaban; they place them in the position of their verbs and let them stand in their place; for this reason they do not use them together with them. The shift from the accusative to the nominative, as inchoative, serves to indicate the stability of the meaning," etc.

It is the habit of eloquent Arabs not to depart from the original form except when they aim at a purpose for which they departed. The shift here from the accusative to the nominative is so that they may indicate permanence and stability through the nominal form of the sentence; the indication of generality derived in context from the generic "al" (al-jinsiyya); and the indication of emphasis derived from fronting. None of these three can be obtained if the verbal noun remained in the accusative, since the accusative indicates the implied verb, and the implied is like the uttered, so the sentence would not be nominal, since the noun in it stands for the verb, so it signifies the implied verb, and so permanence is not obtained. Also, fronting cannot be considered with it, so emphasis is not obtained. And although the combination of the article with the accusative is permitted, as this has been read, and it is the dialect of Tamim, as Sibawayh said, the definiteness then does not indicate generality of all praises, because if the verb is taken as "aḥmadu" with the first-person hamza, it covers only the speaker's praises and not the praises of all people; and if the verb is taken as "naḥmadu" with the nun meaning all believers, by the indication of "ihdina al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm" [1:6] and by the indication of "iyyāka na'budu" [1:5], then it covers only the praises of the believers or of all monotheists. How so, when the People of the Book praised God, Exalted is He, and the Arabs praised Him in the pre-Islamic age? Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"al-ḥamdu lillāhi ḥamdan lā inqiṭā'a lahu / fa-laysa iḥsānuhu 'annā bi-maqṭū'"

"Praise belongs to God, a praise with no end to it; / His kindness toward us is never cut off."

As for when the praise is no longer tied to a verb, the statement becomes about the genus of praise, that it is established for God, and so it covers every praise, as will come.

This is the meaning of what is transmitted from Sibawayh, that he said: whoever puts "al-ḥamd" in the nominative says that praise comes from Him and from all creation; whoever puts it in the accusative says that praise is from Him alone, exalted is He. Know that the accusative reading, though it is irregular (shādhdha), is useful here, because it indicates an Arabic consideration in the development of this well-known construction, and that some Arabs pronounced it in the definite form without forgetting the original absolute object. It has thus become clear that the phrase "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is more eloquent than "al-ḥamda lillāhi" in the accusative, and that "al-ḥamda lillāhi" in the accusative and definite is more eloquent than "ḥamdan lillāhi" in the indefinite. The nominative "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is more eloquent because it signifies permanence and stability.

The Kashshaf says: the shift from the accusative to the nominative indicates the stability and fixity of the meaning, and of it is His saying, exalted is He: "qālū salāman," [11:69] "qāla salāmun," the second salām being in the nominative to indicate that Abraham, peace be upon him, greeted them with a greeting better than theirs. End.

If you say: emphasis falls on praise, though the mention of God's name is more important, so the proper course would be to front God's name and leave praise unemphasized, so as not to resort to changing it from the accusative to the nominative for the sake of that emphasis. I say: praise is fronted because the context here is the context of praise, since it is the beginning of the foremost blessing deserving praise, namely the sending down of the Qur'an, in which lies the success of both abodes. That favor is among the greatest things for which God is praised, among the sublime attributes of perfection, especially since the Qur'an comprises the perfection of meaning, wording, and purpose. So its arising at the beginning of hearing it sent down and the beginning of its recitation reminds one of the lovely attributes of its Sender, Exalted is He, and that reminds of the obligation to praise Him and not to neglect Him. So the context is undoubtedly the context of praise, and for this reason it is fronted, and what would indicate its being delayed is removed from it, since that contradicts emphasis. Then this emphasis is achieved, and the consideration of emphasis is also achieved by fronting it even over the mention of God, Exalted is He, out of regard for the accidental importance of praise in the context, although the mention of God is more important in itself; because accidental importance takes precedence over original importance, since the former is required by the context and situation, while the latter is required by reality. Eloquence is conformity to what the situation and context require. Also, what is emphasized by an accidental cause is the thing most in need of indicating its cause, since it may be hidden, unlike a known and established matter, where there is no benefit in pointing it out, nor does pointing out something else cause it to be lost.

If you say: how can fronting praise, which is an inchoative, indicate emphasis, when it is the original order, and the characteristic of fronting that indicates emphasis is fronting what ought to be delayed?

I say: even if that is granted, the meaning of fronting it is the speaker's intention to bring it first while it was possible to bring it later; for the eloquent have two commonly used forms for praising God: one is "al-ḥamdu lillāh," as in the Fatiha, and the other is "lillāhi al-ḥamd," as in Surat al-Jathiya.

As for the intention of generality, it will become clear when the meaning of the definite article in it is explained. The definiteness in it by "al" is definiteness of the genus, because the verbal noun here is originally a substitute for the verb, so the indicator of the verb and what occupies its place necessarily indicates the genus; when the article enters on it, it is for defining its referent, because the article indicates definiteness of the named; and when the named is a genus, the article indicates its definiteness. The meaning of genus-definiteness is that this genus is known to the hearer: when you say "al-ḥamdu lillāh" or "al-'ajabu laka," you mean that this genus is known to you and to your addressee, and is not confused with anything else, just as when you say "al-rajul" and mean a specific one in the conventional (anaphoric) definiteness, you mean that this one among people is known between you and your addressee; so in meaning it is like the indefinite, in that the definiteness of the genus has no great meaning with it, since the specification of the genus from among the rest of the genera is achieved by mentioning its word, which signifies it by lexical convention, and this suffices for its not indicating anything else; for none of the other genera shares it in the word, nor is there a supposed entry of others alongside it in the addressee's mind. This contrasts with the definiteness of external reference, which indicates one specific individual between you and your addressee from among the rest of the individuals of the genus that the word covers. So this definiteness, namely genus-definiteness, produces nothing beyond confirming the word, establishing it, and clarifying it for the hearer, because you...

"When you have made it a known (referent), you have indicated that it is clear and manifest. This calls for attention to the genus and bringing it close to what is known and famous. This is the meaning of the statement of the author of al-Kashshaf, and it is similar to the definite article in (arsalaha al-'ira'a) [Qur'an 79:1], its meaning being a reference to what everyone knows: what praise is, and what 'ira' is, among the kinds of actions. This is taken from the words of Sibawayh.

The article of definiteness here is not for comprehensiveness (istighraq), because you know that it is the article of the genus (lam al-jins). For this reason the author of al-Kashshaf said: "The comprehensiveness that many people imagine is an illusion on their part. Yet the meaning of comprehensiveness is achieved here by way of implication, because the ruling that the genus of praise is exclusive to Him, the Exalted, arises from the presence of the article of genus in His saying (al-hamdu) and the article of exclusivity in His saying 'lillah' [to Allah], which necessitates that the individual instances of praise are confined to being attached to the name of Allah, the Exalted. For when the genus is exclusive, its individuals are exclusive; for if any individual instance of praise were realized for other than Allah, the genus would be realized within it, and so the meaning of the exclusivity of the genus derived from the particle of exclusivity placed before the Name of Majesty would not be complete. Moreover, this exclusivity is a claimed (ida'i) exclusivity, so it holds the position of a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i) for the sake of emphasis."

The lam in His saying, Exalted is He, "lillah," may be for exclusivity, on the basis that it is a claimed exclusivity as already explained. It may also be the lam of reinforcement, which strengthens the connection of the governing word to its object, since the governing word (a noun deriving from a verb) is weak by reason of its secondary status; the definiteness by the article further weakens it, because it removes it further from resemblance to verbs. The meaning of exclusivity is not lost, because it has already been derived from the definiteness of the two parts.

Furthermore, scholars have differed over whether the sentence "al-hamdu lillah" is a declarative statement (khabar) or a performative utterance (insha'). This has a special connection to tafsir, since it returns to the meaning expressed by the speaker's words: "All praise belongs to Allah." The summary of the matter is that performative speech may arise by transferring a compound from declarative to performative use, as with formulae of contracts such as "I sold" and "I bought," and likewise verbs of praise, blame and hope such as 'asa (perhaps), ni'ma (how excellent) and bi'sa (how wretched). The latter has two types: one used for performative speech while retaining its use for declaration, and one restricted to performative speech.
