The first is like the formulae of contracts, for they are used as declaratives: you say "I sold the house to Zayd," which I informed you that he had bargained with me for; and you say "I sold the house to Zayd" or "I sold you the house for such-and-such," and this is performative by the indication that it came for the purpose of calling witnesses, or by the indication that the declaration is attributed to the addressee while the subject of the report is one of his conditions. The second is like ni'ma and 'asa. Having established this, the scholars have differed over whether "al-hamdu lillah" is a report of the establishment of praise for Allah or the performance of praise of Him, into two positions.

One group holds that it is a declarative statement. Among them are two sub-groups: some claim that it is a declarative that remains declarative, with no indication of performativity in it. This was objected to on the ground that the speaker of it would not then be praising Allah, the Exalted, whereas the intention is that he praises and glorifies Allah, the Exalted. It was answered that a report of praise being established for Him, the Exalted, is an acknowledgment that He is described with beauty, since praise is itself the very description with beauty, and it suffices that this description arises from people and the speaker transmits it.

It may also be answered that the reporter is included in the generality of his report according to the majority of the scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh). It was also answered that the speaker's being a praiser may arise by implication (iltizam) from the declaration. They mean that it is a customary implication, because the matter upon which people have long agreed is one that anyone who knows it follows them in; so the speaker's reporting that he knows this indicates, by custom, that he follows them in it. This is the direction of the implication, though it has remained hidden from many. That is, it is like the arising of an implied benefit from a declarative statement, as established in the science of rhetoric (ma'ani), such as your saying, "You stayed awake last night," meaning that you knew of his staying awake. It does not follow that this is performative, because the estimation on this view is that the speaker reports his being a praiser just as he reports that all people are praisers; thus it is a declaration, not a performative, and what is derived from it by way of implication is also a declarative meaning.

This also is objected to on this estimation: the speaker's praise becomes not intended for its own sake but incidental, whereas the context is the praise of the speaker, not the praise of other people. It was answered that the direct meaning (al-ma'na al-mutabaqi) may be brought for the sake of the implied meaning (al-ma'na al-iltizami), since it is a means to it. Its parallel is the saying of the Arabs, "tall of the sword-belt," meaning tall of stature; for the length of the sword-belt is mentioned in order to indicate the meaning of tallness of stature.

A second group held that "al-hamdu lillah" is necessarily a declarative statement, except that by it is meant performance, while the declarative form is maintained, just as a declarative is used to express lamentation and grief, as in (inni wada'tuha untha) ["Indeed I have given birth to her, a female"] [Qur'an 3:36], and the saying of Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi:

"My passion is with the Yemeni caravan, ascending."

So the primary aim is performance, but the shift to declarative form is for what is achieved through the declarative form of signifying comprehensiveness, exclusivity, permanence and stability. The link between a declaration about people's praise and the performance of praise is clear from what you have learned of the link on the first account; indeed it is more evident here, because one who reports the praise of people to Allah, the Exalted, is without doubt performing praise of Him through that. That the implied meaning in metonymy is the intended one, rather than the direct meaning, is more evident than in the view of pure declaration, because what is known of metonymy is that it is an expression whose intended meaning is the implied meaning of its sense, while the original meaning may also be intended along with it. This shows that the original meaning is either not intended, or intended incidentally, since "ma'a" [with] introduces the dependent (matbu').

The second position is that "al-hamdu lillah" is pure performance, with no indication of declarativeness, being among the formulae that the Arabs transferred from declaration to the performance of praise, just as they transferred the formulae of contracts and the verbs of praise and blame; that is, a transfer while the declarative meaning is not extinguished in usage. For you may say "al-hamdu lillah" in answer to one who says, "To whom belongs praise?" or "Whom shall I praise?" But the retention of the original meaning is weak and so requires a context. The truth from which there is no escape is that "al-hamdu lillah" is a declarative used in performance; the intention is performativity without doubt, but it has been turned to declarative form so that the sentence of praise may carry such particularities as befit the majesty of the one praised: indication of permanence, stability, comprehensiveness, exclusivity and emphasis. None of these can be achieved by a performative form such as "hamdan lillah" or "ahmadu Allaha hamdan." That the Arabs regarded it as performative and not declarative is shown by the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"And when she ran in the fuel like the gleam of dawn, we produced for its Creator thanks."

He expressed the mention of the word praise or thanks by "producing" (ahdatha), and "producing" is synonymous with performance linguistically; so his saying "ahdatha" is a declarative which relates what he expressed by "producing," namely his praise occurring at the moment of its blazing in the firewood.

Allah is the proper name of the Essence, the Necessarily Existent, the One deserving of all praises. The origin of this name is al-Ilah with the definite article, which is the definition of ilah, a common noun for the worshipped, derived from alaha (with a fatha on the lam) meaning 'abada (worshipped), or from aliha (with a kasra on the lam) meaning tahayyara (was bewildered), or sakana (was tranquil), or faza'a (was alarmed), or wulia (was infatuated), which returns to a meaning that necessarily involves submission and veneration. It is thus fi'al with a kasra on the first letter in the sense of maf'ul, like kitab. The Arabs applied it to every worshipped thing among their idols, because they regarded them as truly deserving of worship. For this reason they made its plural ālihah on the pattern af'ilah, with the second hamza lightened into a long vowel. I suppose that the name of Him, Exalted is He, was established in the language of the Arabs before the entry of polytheism among them, so its original imposition indicated His being singled out for divinity, since there is no ilah other than Him. Therefore it became a proper name for Him. This is not a proper name by predominance (al-'alam bi'l-ghalaba) but a proper name by restriction, like al-shams and al-qamar (the sun and the moon). There is nothing strange in its being both a common noun and a proper name. For this reason they meant by it the worshipped in truth, as a refutation of the people of polytheism, before polytheism entered among the Arabs. We have not found that the Arabs used al-Ilah with the article, singular, of any of their idols; they rather added it to a possessor, saying "ilah of the Banu so-and-so," and most often they said "rabb of the Banu so-and-so," or they used the plural, as they said to 'Abd al-Muttalib, "Lord of the gods" (ard al-alihah). In the hadith of the conquest of Mecca: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) found the gods in the House.

When al-Ilah became restricted to the one necessarily existent God, they derived for Him a proper name from the common noun, to add to the indication that He is the one worthy of this name, so that the name would be specific to Him, not permissible to apply to other than Him, following the custom of personal proper names. I think they were inventive and wondrous when they made the proper name of His Essence, Exalted is He, derived from the common noun that indicates the concept of divinity, as an alert that His Essence, Exalted is He, is not evoked in the mind of the first coiner of this name, the first speaker of this name among the people of the tongue, except with the attribute of divinity; and as an alert that He, Exalted is He, is the most worthy of being deified and worshipped, because He is the Creator of all. They dropped the hamza from al-Ilah because this word was used very frequently in indicating Him, Exalted is He, just as they dropped the hamza of al-Unas, saying al-nas (the people). For this reason they restored it in some speech.

Al-Ba'ith ibn Hurayth said:

"Ma'adh al-Ilah that she be like a gazelle, nor a doll, nor a noble fawn of the white-antelope."

Just as they restored the hamza of al-Unas in the saying of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras al-Asadi:

"Indeed the deaths will look down on the people who are safe."

This word, in its third stage, took the place of personal proper names, so they handled it in this way to move with it to a new stage, making it like a new proper name. This method is followed in some proper names.

Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni said in his commentary on the saying of Ta'abbata Sharran in the thirteenth poem of al-Hamasa:

"Indeed I am one who spreads my praise, aiming with it at the son of the paternal uncle of truthfulness, Shams ibn Malik."

Shams with a damma on the shin, and its origin is Shams with a fatha, as they said Hujr and Sulma; so it is among those changed from their counterparts for the sake of being a proper name. End of quote.

In al-Kashshaf, in the tafsir of the surah of Abu Lahab, after mentioning that some readers recited "Abi Lahb" with a sukun on the ha', it says verbatim: "This is from the changing of proper names, like their saying Shums ibn Malik with a damma." End of quote. And before that it says: "Fulayta ibn Qasim, the amir of Mecca, had two sons, one called 'Abd Allah in the genitive, and the other 'Abd Allah in the accusative, and in Mecca there was a man called 'Abd Allah who was known only in this way." End of quote. He means with a kasra on the dal of 'Abd in all its cases of inflection. So by this indication it is a particular kind of proper name, namely one stronger than a proper name by predominance, because it has a new form after the predominant form.

This method in the proper naming that befell the name Allah has no parallel among proper names, so His name, Exalted is He, is unlike the names of created things, just as the entity of that name is unlike the entities of the names of created things. They indicated their forgetting of the definiteness in the alif and lam, and that they made them part of the word, by permitting the vocative of the name Allah while retaining the alif and lam, so they say "Ya Allah," even though they forbid the vocative of what has the alif and lam.

**[Page 165]**

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) cited the verse of al-Bu'ayth, quoted earlier, as evidence that the origin of the name is *al-Ilah*. His commentators did not explain how this verse serves as proof. It is a sound argument, because *ma'adh* is one of the verbal nouns that in their usage never occurs with a genitive other than the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalala*, "Allah"), like *subhan*. It has therefore come to function like proverbial expressions in being bound to this construction, and one says *ma'adh Allah* ("God forbid"). When the poet says *ma'adh al-Ilah*, and he is one of the eloquent speakers of the language, we know that they regard *al-Ilah* as the origin of the word *Allah*. For this reason, this alteration is not a change, but merely a variation in the letters of a single word, like the differences in the modes of pronunciation while the word remains one. Do you not see that they cited

**[Page 165, continued]**

as evidence that *Lah* is a lightened form of *Allah*, the verse of Dhu al-Usba' al-'Adwani:

*Lah* is the son of your paternal uncle; you have not surpassed me in lineage,
nor are you my judge so that you may subdue me.

And by their saying *lah abuka* ("by God, your father"), because this is something that remains in one fixed form, for they say *lillah abuka*, *lillah ibnu 'ammika* and *lillah anta*.

Other opinions have been mentioned concerning the origin of the Name of Majesty. Among them: its origin is *lah*, the verbal noun of *laha yalihu layhan*, meaning "to be concealed"; the name was applied to God Most High, and then the definite article *al-* was added to it to indicate the origin, as with *al-fadl* and *al-majd* as proper names. Al-Jawhari reported this view from Sibawayh, saying that he permitted it. Another is that its origin is *Wilah* with a *waw*, on the pattern *fi'al* in the sense of *maf'ul*, from *waliha* ("to be bewildered"). The *waw* was then changed to a hamza because the kasra upon it was considered heavy, as in *i'a'* and *ishah*, meaning *wi'a'* and *wishah* ("container" and "sash"). It was then defined by *al-* and the hamza was deleted. Another is that its origin is *Laha*, which in Syriac is a name for Him, Most High, and it was Arabized by deleting the *alif* and adding the *lam* to it. Another is that it is a proper name established for the Name of Majesty as a primary designation, without being derived from *allaha* and made into *al-Ilah*; its resemblance in form to our saying *al-Ilah* is therefore an accidental and unintended similarity. This view was held by a group including al-Zajjaj, and it is attributed to al-Khalil and Sibawayh. Some scholars justified it by saying that the Arabs did not leave anything without giving it a word, so how could they have left unnamed a name of His, Most High, upon which His attributes could be predicated?

The *lam* of the Name of Majesty is necessarily pronounced with emphasis (*tafkhim*) when the letter before it is not vowelled with kasra. Some writers attempted to justify this with arguments that are not free from objection. For this reason, the author of al-Kashshaf refused to dwell on it, and said: "All the Arabs agree upon it (i.e., the emphatic pronunciation), and their unanimity upon it is evidence that they inherited it from one generation to the next."

The reason the predicate in the prepositional phrase, which contains the Name of Majesty, was not placed before the subject, so that one would say *lillahi al-hamd*, is that the subject here is praise for the revelation of the Qur'an and for the honour of Islam, and these two are a favour from God Most High. Thus He praised Himself for them at the beginning of the recitation of the Book through which the people's welfare in both abodes is achieved. Therefore the context called for emphasis upon it, in consideration of the contingent importance of praise, even though the mention of God is more important in its essence. Yet contingent importance takes precedence over essential importance, as the circumstance and context require.

Eloquence is precisely the pursuit of what the circumstance requires. Moreover, since praise is connected to the Name of God, Most High, emphasis upon it is also emphasis upon the affairs of God, Most High.

**[Page 166]**

Among the most astonishing opinions is what was mentioned by the author of *al-Manhal al-Asfa fi Sharh al-Shifa*, al-Tilimsani, from a group of scholars: that the Name of Majesty should be refrained from discussing as to its meaning, out of glorification and reverence, and because discussing it depends upon the permission of the Lawgiver.

* * *

***Rabb al-'alamin*** (Lord of the worlds)

This is a qualifier of the Name of Majesty. Having attributed praise to the Name of His Essence, Most High, as an indication of essential deservingness, it then followed with the qualifier, which is *al-Rabb* (the Lord), so that praise would also be connected to this attribute, because the qualifier of the object of a relation is also related. For this reason, He did not say *al-hamdu li-rabbi al-'alamin*, as He said: ﴿The day when people will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6], so as to indicate that He also deserves praise through His attribute, just as He deserves it through His Essence. He predicated four attributes of Him: *Rabb al-'alamin*, *al-Rahman*, *al-Rahim*, and *Malik yawm al-din*, to announce His attributive deservingness. The mention of these names, which convey attributes, indicates an intention to consider their original meanings. This is among the things derived from speech by way of implication (*istitba'*), because when mention of the attribute suffices without mention of the thing attributed, especially when the attribute has been made to function as a proper name, as with His attributes, Most High, and when mention of the word for the thing attributed also suffices as an indication of the deservingness of praise, which is the purpose of the sentence, we know that the speaker combined the two only to indicate that both meanings, of the attributed and of the attribute, are worthy of being the object of praise. Moreover, mention of His attributes specific to Him includes a reminder of what distinguishes Him from the supposed gods of the nations, such as idols, images, and elements, as will come later at His saying, Most High: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fatiha: 4].

*Al-Rabb* is either a verbal noun or an adjective of the form *fa'l*, from *rabbahu yarubbuhu*, meaning *rabbahu* ("he raised him" / "he nurtured him"), so that *rabb* means *murabbi* (one who nurtures) and *sa'is* (one who manages).

Tarbiyah (nurturing) is bringing a thing gradually to its perfection. It may also be derived from *rabbahu* meaning "he owned him" (*malakahu*). If it is a verbal noun on both interpretations, then its use as a descriptor is for emphasis, which is clear. If it is an adjective in both interpretations, then it comes according to the rare patterns of the adjective, since the pattern *fa'l* from *fa'ala yaf'ulu* is found only rarely; among these is the saying *namma al-hadith yanummuhu*, so that *fahuwa nammun li-l-hadith* ("he is a tale-bearer of the speech").

The more evident view is that it is derived from *rabbahu* in the sense of *rabbahu* ("he raised him") and *sasahu* ("he managed him"), not from *rabbahu* in the sense of "he owned him," because the first is more suitable to the context here, since the intended meaning is that He is the Manager of creatures, the Director of their affairs, and the one who brings them to the utmost of their perfection. Also, if it were understood in the sense of "owner," then His saying after that: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fatiha: 4] would be like an emphasis, and emphasis departs from the original, and there is no need for it here, unless it is answered that *al-'alamin* includes only the worlds of this life, so it needs to clarify that He owns the Hereafter as He owns this world. Although the most common usage in the speech of the Arabs is that *al-Rabb* means *al-Malik* (the King) and *al-Sayyid* (the Lord/Master), and this is what prompted the author of al-Kashshaf to limit it to the meaning of "master" and "king," and he permitted in it the two possibilities of being a verbal noun and an adjective, yet the contextual evidence may turn the word away from its most frequent usages toward a lesser meaning, for both usages are well known, whether literal or figurative. The occasional understanding arising from the particular context does not mean that the word is understood in that meaning in all its occurrences, as is not hidden.

The Arabs did not restrict the word *al-Rabb* to God, Most High, neither absolutely nor with qualification, due to what you know of its pattern and derivation. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

*He is the Lord and the Witness over the Day of al-Hiyarayn, and the trial is a trial.*

He means 'Amr ibn Hind. And al-Nabigha said about al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith:

*You hasten to al-Nu'man until you reach him,
ransom for you from a lord, my wealth and my heritage.*

And he said about al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir when he fell ill:

*And a lord, may God make his deed good,
and he was for the creatures a helper.*

The author of al-Kashshaf and those who followed him said that it was not applied to anyone other than God, Most High, except with qualification, or else they produced no proof for that. But I have seen that the usage is otherwise. As for its application to each of their gods, there is no doubt about it, as Ghawi ibn Zalim or 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

*Is a lord one over whose head the foxes urinate?
Indeed, he is humiliated, the one upon whom the foxes have urinated.*

And they named al-'Uzza *al-Rabbah* (the female lord). Its plural *arbab* is the strongest evidence that it is applied to more than one, so how could the claim that its application among them was restricted to God, Most High, be valid? As for its application as a construct or linked to a specific referent, its frequent occurrence is evident, as in *rabb al-dar* (master of the house), *rabb al-Furs* (master of the Persians), and *rabb Bani Fulan* (lord of the clan of so-and-so).

The application has also occurred in Islam, when He related of Yusuf, peace be upon him, his saying: ﴿Indeed, he is my lord; he has made my dwelling good﴾ [Yusuf: 23], if the pronoun refers to the Aziz. Likewise His saying: ﴿Are lords dispersed better?﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. This is an application of *rabb*, both construct and non-construct, to other than God, Most High, in Islam; for the word is Arabic, and it was applied in Islam, and it was not Yusuf who used this word, but rather he used its synonym. So if it were not valid to express by this word the meaning Yusuf expressed, there would be in the other words of Arabic a substitute. What was reported in the hadith is only the prohibition against anyone saying to his master *rabbi* ("my lord"), and that he should say *sayyidi* ("my master"). This is a prohibition of disapproval for the sake of discipline. For this reason the prohibition was specified only when the genitive is one who is customarily worshipped, such as the names of people, to avert the suspicion of association (*shirk*) and to cut off its root. They allowed one to say *rabb al-dabba* (master of the animal) and *rabb al-dar* (master of the house). But as for its unqualified use, the disapproval is stronger, so no one should say of the king or the like: "This is a *rabb*."

*Al-'alamin* is the plural of *'alam*. They said that the pattern *fa'al* was not pluralized in this way except in two words: *'alam* and *yasam*, the name of the flower known as jasmine. It is said they pluralized it as *yasamun* and *yasamin*. Al-A'sha said:

*And the *jull* and the *yasam* met us,
and the *musmi'at* and its butcher.*

*Al-'alam* is a genus among the genera of existent things. The Arabs formed it on the pattern *fa'al* with a fatha on the 'ayn, derived from *'ilm* (knowledge) or *'alamah* (sign), because every genus has a distinction from others, so it is a sign for it; or it is the cause of knowledge of it, so that it is not confused with other things.

This pattern is specifically used, for the most part, to indicate an instrument, like *khatim* (seal), *qalib* (mould), and *tabi'* (stamp). So they made the worlds, because they are like instruments for knowledge of the Creator, or for knowledge of realities. The Arabs were masterful in this subtle point when they formed the name of the genus of created things on the pattern *fa'il*, for this reason; and they were masterful when they pluralized it as the plural of rational beings, even though some of it is not rational, giving precedence to the rational.

Al-Taftazani said in his commentary on al-Kashshaf: "*al-'alam* is a name for those who possess knowledge and for every genus by which the Creator is known; one says *'alam al-mulk* (the world of dominion), *'alam al-insan* (the world of humanity), *'alam al-nabat* (the world of plants)." He means that it is not used in the singular except when qualified by a type that specifies it; one says *'alam al-ins* (the world of humankind), *'alam al-hayawan* (the world of animals), *'alam al-nabat* (the world of plants). It is not a name for the totality of what is other than Him, Most High, such that it would have a collective sense making its pluralization impermissible. This is the precise linguistic analysis, for it is not found in the speech of the Arabs that *'alam* is applied to the totality of what is other than God, Most High. It was applied to this sense only by the scholars of kalam in their saying "the world is created," so it is a technical term.

The definite article in it is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*), by contextual evidence of the rhetorical situation. For when there is no external specific reference, and no meaning for taking it as the nature of the thing or as a mentally known referent, then the article is purely for comprehensiveness of all individuals, to avoid arbitrariness. Its comprehensiveness is the comprehensiveness of genera, which necessarily applies to them. This is the meaning of the saying of the author of al-Kashshaf, "so that it encompasses every genus named by it." However, the comprehensiveness of genera necessarily entails the comprehensiveness of their individuals, a clear implication, since genera are not intended in themselves, especially in a context of ruling by lordship over them, for there is no sense in the lordship of realities.

The word *al-'alam* was pluralized and not used in the singular because the plural is evidence of comprehensiveness. For if it were used in the singular, it would be suspected that the definite article indicated either a known referent or the genus; so the plural was an explicit statement of comprehensiveness. This is the customary practice of plurals with the comprehensive *al-*, according to verification. Since plurality became evidence of comprehensiveness, the sense of collective groups was removed from it, so that the comprehensiveness of plurals is equal to, or more inclusive than, the comprehensiveness of singulars.

And there was refuted what was widespread among the followers of al-Sakkaki, the saying: "the comprehensiveness of the singular is more inclusive," as we will explain at His saying, Most High: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqara: 31].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 1, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

Two epithets derived from the root R-H-M. In the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi, on the authority of Ibn al-Anbari, on the authority of al-Mubarrad, it is stated that al-Rahman is a Hebrew word that was transferred into Arabic. He said: its origin is with the marked kha' (خ), and its kha' was then replaced by an unmarked ha' (ح) according to most of the Arabs, as is the way of alteration in arabization. He cited in support of this the verse of Jarir addressing al-Akhtal:

"Will you abandon, for the priest, your migration and the wiping of your backs, [and] the crouching camels (rakhaman qurbana)?"

The transmitted reading is with the marked kha' (خ). Al-Mubarrad did not bring any proof for what he claimed. And why should al-Rahman not be Arabic, just as it was Hebrew? Arabic and Hebrew are sister languages, and it may well be that original Arabic is older than Hebrew. Perhaps what emboldened him to claim that al-Rahman is a Hebrew word is what the Qur'an related of the polytheists in His saying: ﴿They said, "And what is the Most Gracious?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]. This implies that the Arabs did not know this name as a name of God, as will come. Some Yemeni Arabs say rakhima rukhmatan, with the marked letter.

The noun "mercy" (rahma) is established in the Arabic language for the tenderness and inclination of the heart toward a living being, such that it moves the one characterized by it to gentleness toward the one shown mercy, to doing good to him, to removing harm from him, and to helping him against hardships.

It is therefore among the psychological states, because it is an affection (infi'al). And this state has an impulse that moves its bearer to existential actions, according to his capacity and in proportion to the strength of his affection. The origin of mercy is from the category of affection (infi'al), and its effects are from the category of action (fi'l). So when someone is described as merciful, its meaning is that the aforementioned affection occurs within him; and when it is reported of him that he "had mercy on" another, it means that an effect of the effects of mercy proceeded from him, since the verb raḥima can only be transitive to the one shown mercy in this sense. Thus the quiddity of mercy has no existential particulars, but rather particulars of its effects.

The description of God Most High with attributes of mercy in languages arises in accordance with the beliefs of their speakers regarding what is permissible and impossible for God. Most nations were anthropomorphist, and then this comes
صفحة ١٧٠
into the language of the revealed laws as an expression of lofty meanings with the utmost that languages permit, together with the belief in God's transcendence above the accidents of created beings, by the general proof of transcendence, which is the content of the Qur'anic statement: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. So the people of faith, when they hear or utter the two epithets al-Rahman al-Rahim, do not understand from them the occurrence of that affection which is noted in the reality of mercy in the common usage of the Arabic language, because the proofs of God's transcendence above accidents are manifest. Rather, what is intended by this description, with respect to God Most High, is the affirmation of the supreme purpose of the reality of mercy, namely the proceeding of the effects of mercy: gentleness, kindness, beneficence, and aid. For what lies beyond that, of the conditions noted in the meaning of mercy in people's usage, has no importance except that its effects cannot occur among them without it. Do you not see that a person may have mercy on someone yet cannot benefit him, due to incapacity or the like?

Abu Hamid al-Ghazali has alluded to what we have said in al-Maqsad al-Asna, with his words: "One who wishes to fulfil the need of the needy but does not fulfil it: if he is able to fulfil it, he is not called merciful, since if the wish were complete he would have fulfilled it; and if he is incapable, he may be called merciful in consideration of the mercy and tenderness that affect him, but he is deficient." From this you know that applying such a description to God Most High is not among the ambiguous (mutashabih), because the intended meaning is evident through its frequent usage, and the exclusion of God from the implications of the meaning in its conventional sense, of what is not fitting to God's majesty, is certain. Just as we apply "the Knowing" (al-'Alim) to God while being certain that His knowledge is free of need for reflection and inference and of prior ignorance, and as we apply "the Living" (al-Hayy) to Him while being certain that His life is free of habit and becoming, and we apply "the Powerful" (al-Qadir) while being certain that His power is free of treatment and assistance.

Thus the description of Him Most High as al-Rahman al-Rahim belongs to the legally transferred terms (al-manqulat al-shar'iyya), for the Qur'an affirmed God's mercy in His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156]. It is therefore transferred in the language of the Law to the will of God to convey benefaction to His creatures in this world. Most of the Most Beautiful Names are of this kind. As for the ambiguous, it is that whose indication of the transcendent meaning is stronger and more intense. This will come in Surah Al 'Imran at His saying Most High: ﴿and others are ambiguous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. The view taken by the author of al-Kashshaf and many of the verifiers is that al-Rahman is an adjective in the form of the sifa mushabbaha (quality noun), like ghadban, and he exemplified it so in al-Kashshaf. The verb raḥima, though transitive, and the sifa mushabbaha are normally formed from an intransitive verb; however, when a transitive verb becomes like a disposition (sajiyya) of its subject, it takes the place of verbs of natural disposition, so it is changed from fa'ala (with fatha or kasra in the 'ayn) to fa'ula (with damma in the 'ayn), to indicate that it has become a disposition, as they said faqiha al-rajul, zarufa, and fahima. Then the sifa mushabbaha is derived from it after that. Similar examples are numerous in speech. This transformation is recognized by one of two things:
صفحة ١٧١
either by hearing the transformed verb, such as faqiha, or by the existence of its effect, which is the sifa mushabbaha, such as baligh when eloquence has become a disposition for him, while rarely or never having heard balugha. From this comes raḥmān, since raḥuma with damma was not heard. Some grammarians refused that al-Rahman be a sifa mushabbaha, on the basis that the derived verb from which it is formed is transitive; and Ibn Malik inclined to this in his commentary on al-Tashil, in the chapter on the sifa mushabbaha, and he compared it to rabb and malik. As for al-Rahim, Sibawayh held that it is among the patterns of intensity (mubalagha), and it remains indicating transitivity; while the author of al-Kashshaf and the majority did not establish the pattern fa'il among the patterns of intensity, so al-Rahim according to them is also a sifa mushabbaha, like marid and saqim, and the intensity is present in it under both considerations. The truth is what Sibawayh held. There is no disagreement among the people of language that both epithets indicate intensity in the attribute of mercy, that is, its firmness and its connection to many of those shown mercy. The disagreement is only about the manner in which intensity is derived from them, and whether they are synonymous in describing the attribute of mercy or there is a difference between them. The truth is that the derivation of intensity is obtained through tracing usage, and that usage proceeded according to a principle observed by the founders of the language: increasing the form to intend an increase in the meaning of the root. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "They say that the increase in the structure is for an increase in meaning." Al-Zajjaj said of al-Ghadban: "he is the one filled with anger." Among the Arabs' witticisms that resounded in my ear: they call one of their vehicles al-shuqdhuf, which is a light conveyance, not as heavy as the Iraqi litters. So I said to a man of them on the road to al-Ta'if, meaning the Iraqi litter: "What is the name of this litter?" He said: "Is its name not al-shiqindaf?" I said: "Yes." He said: "This is its name, al-shiqindaf," so he increased the structure of the name for the increase of the named thing. This is a general rule that does not fail except in known additions made to yield a new meaning without increasing the meaning of the root itself, such as the addition of the diminutive yā', for it added a meaning beyond the root's basic meaning and is not an increase in the root's meaning. As for something like ḥadhir, which is among the patterns of intensity and has fewer letters than ḥādhir, it is among the exceptions to the rule, since the rule is a general tendency.

After it has become established that each of the two epithets al-Rahman and al-Rahim indicates intensity in God Most High's attribution of mercy, most scholars have said that al-Rahman is more emphatic than al-Rahim, on the basis that increase in form indicates increase in meaning. Toward this view inclined the majority of verifiers, such as Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn Jinni, al-Zajjaj, and al-Zamakhshari. Upon this principle, namely that increase in form indicates increase in meaning, there has widely arisen a difficulty regarding the sequence of describing Him as al-Rahman followed by describing Him as al-Rahim, although it is the practice of the people of eloquence, when they apply two epithets with one meaning to a subject in a state of perfection, to ascend from the more general to the more specific, and from the strong to the stronger, as in the saying: "brave and courageous," "generous and bountiful," "a learned, skilled scholar," "an eloquent orator," "a superb poet."
صفحة ١٧٢
Many answers have been given by the exegetes concerning the justification of ascending from al-Rahman to al-Rahim, and their return is to considering al-Rahman more specific than al-Rahim; so following the first with the second is a generalization after a specific. For this reason the description al-Rahman is restricted to Him Most High, and its first application was among what the Qur'an specifically singled Him out with, in verification, such that the description by it was not known among the Arabs, as will come.

The meaning of al-Rahim is that mercy is very widely connected, since it is of the forms of intensity; for this reason it is applied to others than God Most High, as in His saying concerning His Messenger: ﴿to the believers he is kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawba: 128]. So mention of one of the two attributes does not suffice without the other. And the precedence of al-Rahman over al-Rahim is because the form indicating essential attribution is more deserving of precedence in description than the attribute indicating multiplicity of its objects.

It is attributed to Qutrub that al-Rahman and al-Rahim indicate one meaning of the sifa mushabbaha, so they are equal, and the combining of them in the verse was made a case of lexical emphasis (al-tawkid al-lafzi). Al-Zajjaj inclined to this, but it is a weak view, since emphasis is contrary to the original, and substantiation (al-ta'sis) is better than emphasis, and the context here is far from the requirement of emphasis. Various reasons have been given for combining the two attributes, but none is convincing.

Most of the leading scholars have mentioned that the description al-Rahman was not used in Arabic speech before Islam, and that the Qur'an is what brought it as an attribute of God Most High; for this reason it was specialized to Him Most High, to the point that it was said it is a proper name for Him and not an attribute. They proved this by His saying Most High: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Gracious," they say, "And what is the Most Gracious?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 60], and His saying: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Gracious﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30]. Similar to these two verses are repeated in the Qur'an, especially in the Meccan surahs such as Surah al-Furqan and Surah al-Mulk. The name al-Rahman is mentioned in Surah al-Mulk by its apparent name and its pronoun eight times, which conveys concern with establishing this name for God Most High in the hearts of the hearers. The apparent view is that this description had been forgotten in their speech, or that they denied that it is among the names of God.

Among the subtleties of the Qur'an is that it chose the name al-Rahman in His saying: ﴿None holds them up except the Most Gracious﴾ [al-Mulk: 19] in Surah al-Mulk, and He said: ﴿None holds them up except God﴾ [al-Nahl: 79] in Surah al-Nahl, since the verse of Surah al-Mulk is Meccan, and the verse of Surah al-Nahl is a portion of that surah revealed at Medina. As for the verse of one of the poets of Banu Hanifa about Musaylima:

"You have risen to glory, O son of the most noble fathers, and you are the rain of mankind; may you never cease to be al-Rahman."

He said it after the coming of Islam and during the apostasy of the people of al-Yamama, and they had given Musaylima at that time the title "Rahman of al-Yamama," and that was from their extremism in disbelief.

And the placing of these two exalted attributes after the name of majesty (al-jalala)
صفحة ١٧٣

The lordship (ruboobiyyah) is described as being "Lord of the worlds" because of an evident connection for the eloquent reader. After Allah is described with what necessarily entitles Him to praise, namely that He is Lord of the worlds, meaning the one who manages their affairs and brings them to their perfection in both the physical and the spiritual existence, it is fitting to follow this with His description as al-Raḥmān (the Most Merciful). Mercy is an essential attribute of His, from which its effects proceed in a general and constant manner, as was mentioned earlier. Since He is Lord of the worlds and those who are nurtured are weak, their need for mercy is clear, and their expectation of it from the One who is essentially characterized by it is well founded.

If you ask: lordship already requires mercy, since it is bringing a thing to its perfection gradually, and that comprises all blessings, so why is it necessary to mention that He is al-Raḥmān? I say: mercy implies that this bringing to perfection was not done in a way of hardship, but with care for what suits each kind and each individual and fits its capacity and readiness. Thus lordship is a blessing, and a blessing may be attained through some kind of hardship and harm. So He follows this with the description al-Raḥmān, as an alert that these great blessings reached us by way of gentleness, ease, and the removal of hardship, even in the rulings of obligations, prohibitions, and deterrents, for these are accompanied by ease to the extent that does not nullify their purpose. Most of His management of us is manifest mercy, such as enabling us to use the earth and facilitating its benefits. Among it is His mercy in observing ease to the extent possible, such as obligations that return to our benefit, like purification and the spreading of noble morals. And among it is what benefits the majority, which is followed by the mercy of all, since in the mercy toward the majority there is mercy toward the rest in the ordering of affairs, such as zakat.

It has been disputed whether the word raḥmān, if it is not joined with the definite article (al-), is subject to ṣarf (full inflection, i.e. taking tanwīn) or is prevented from ṣarf (diptote). In al-Kāfiyah (a grammatical treatise by Ibn al-Ḥājib) it is said: when the nūn and alif (of the -ān ending) are in an adjective, the condition for its being prevented from ṣarf is the absence of the feminine form faʿlānah, and it was said that the condition is the presence of faʿlā. On this basis it has been disputed regarding raḥmān. The Banū Asad inflect all faʿlān forms, because they say for every feminine that has a faʿlānah form... [and] al-Zamakhsharī, al-Raḍī, and Ibn Mālik chose that it not be inflected.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 1, verse 4:**

﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾

The following of the three preceding attributes with this one is not merely a list of His attributes, may He be exalted. Rather, it is something raised by the preceding attributes. When He was described as ﴿Lord of the worlds, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, and this was conducive to what we have already mentioned, namely the alerting to the perfection of His gentleness toward those He nurtures in all their states, and then the alerting that His disposal of the existents and their conditions is a disposal of mercy according to the one who reflects, and among those dispositions were the dispositions of command and prohibition, expressed as legislation aimed at preserving the interests of people in general and in particular, and most of that legislation involves removing the accountable person from the call of desire that suits him to follow, and turning him away from it involves compulsion and hardship for him, it was feared that these preceding attributes in the Opening of the Book might lighten for the accountable people the burden of disobedience to what they were commanded, and stir up their hopes for pardon in spite of their making light of that, and that greed might overcome them so that they rely on what they know of the Lordship and the established mercy, and thus do not fear the calamity of turning away from the obligations. Therefore it was required by the context that it be followed by mention that He is the possessor of judgement on the Day of Recompense, the Day when every soul is recompensed for what it has earned, because recompense for an act is a cause for compliance and avoidance, for the preservation of the interests of the world. This was surrounded by promise and threat, and the realisation of that recompense was made to be on the Day of Resurrection. For this reason the attribute of "Malik" or "Malik" (possessor) was chosen here, joined to "the Day of Judgement".

As for "Malik" (king), it indicates the establishment of justice and the absence of leniency in it, because it is the nature of a king to manage the welfare of his subjects and to protect them, and for this reason people appointed kings over themselves. Had it been said "Lord of the Day of Judgement", there would have been an opening for the corrupters, who would find in the Lord's nature mercy and forgiveness. As for "Malik" (possessor), it is like that in its indication of the establishment of recompense in the most suitable of its modes according to the deeds for which one is recompensed.

If you say: since the continuation of the preceding attributes indicates that all of God's dispositions toward us are mercy, that is sufficient to urge compliance and submission, for a person does not oppose what is mercy to him, and so he will inevitably be led to the Law by his own choice. I say: the addressees are of degrees. Among them is he who is not guided to understanding that except after the mention of those attributes is followed by this attribute, and among them is he who is guided to understanding it but thinks that doing what suits him is also mercy toward him, so he may prefer the suitable mercy over the disagreeable mercy even though the latter is beneficial to him. And perhaps he interprets mercy as being a mercy to the public, and that he receives from it only a weak portion, so he prefers the mercy of his particular share over the mercy of his share which follows the general.

And perhaps he interprets that mercy in God's obligations is a generally prevailing matter, not a constant one, and that the attribute of Him as "al-Rahman" with respect to other than legislation, such as creation, provision and giving life, is so. And perhaps he thinks that mercy is in the outcome, so he prefers the immediate thing that suits him. And perhaps he knows all the interests that the obligations contain constantly, but his desire has overpowered him and his wretchedness has prevailed over him.

So all of these are liable to turn away from the legal obligations, and for people like them the following of the preceding attributes with this attribute came as a reminder to them of what recompense will occur on the Day of Reckoning, lest the purpose of legislation be corrupted when every interpreter who wastes it grasps it with his understanding.

[Page 175]

Furthermore, in the following of His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2] and ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Fatiha: 3] with His saying ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ there is an indication that He is the one who holds the disposal in this world and the Hereafter, so this is then a completion. As for His saying "Maliki" (Malik), most readers read it without an alif after the mim, and 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf read "Maliki" (Malik) with an alif. The first is an adjectival form (sifa mushabbaha) which has become a noun for the owner of kingship, with a dammah on the mim, and the second is an active participle from malaka, when one is characterised by possession, with a kasrah on the mim. Both are derived from malaka. The root of the word malaka in the language, its inflections return to the meaning of tightening and controlling, as Ibn 'Atiyya said. Then that is used in literal and figurative senses, in verification and in consideration. The reading "Malik" without an alif indicates the depiction of a state in the hearts of the listeners, because "malik" (with a fatha on the mim and a kasrah on the lam) is the one who has kingship (mulk, with a dammah on the mim), and mulk is more specific than milk (possession), since mulk with a dammah on the mim is the disposal of existing things and taking control, and it is specific to managing the affairs of rational beings and governing their masses, individuals and places, so one says "malik al-nas" (king of the people) and one does not say "malik al-dawabb" (king of the animals) or "al-darahim" (of the dirhams). As for milk with a kasrah on the mim, it is the particular attachment to things and their benefits, to the exclusion of others.

The majority read "Malik" with a fatha on the mim and a kasrah on the lam without an alif, and this reading is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) and his two companions Abu Bakr and 'Umar in the book of al-Tirmidhi. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Abu 'Ali related from some readers that the first to read "Malik yawm al-din" was Marwan ibn al-Hakam, and Abu Bakr ibn al-Sarraj rejected this by saying that the reports that have come refute that. Perhaps the one who said that meant that he was the first to recite it in a particular land. As for the reading "Maliki" with an alif after the mim, in the pattern of the active participle, it is the reading of 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Khalaf, and it is narrated from 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Talha and al-Zubayr, and al-Tirmidhi related in his book that the Prophet (ﷺ) and his two companions also recited with it. Both are sound and established, as is the case with the mutawatir readings (qira'at), as was mentioned in the sixth introduction. The commentators and the argumentative scholars of the readings have taken up the task of explaining what is specific to each of the reading "Malik" without an alif and the reading "Malik" with an alif, by restricting attention to the concept of the word malik and the concept of the word malik, and they neglected the word's being added to "the Day of Judgement". As for the word being added to "the Day of Judgement", both are equal in indicating that He is the one who disposes of the affairs of that day, without the doubt of a partner.

There is no escape from considering an extension in the addition of malik or malik to a day, by interpreting it as the affairs of the Day of Judgement. Moreover, "malik" is a dialect form of "malik" (both meaning possessor of kingship), for in the Qamus: "wa ka-amir wa ka-katif wa ka-sahib: dhu al-mulk" (and like amir, katif and sahib: one who has kingship).

[Page 176]

The Day of Judgement is the Day of Resurrection and the beginning of the Abode of the Hereafter, and "al-din" in it means recompense. Al-Find al-Zimmani said:

"When evil became manifest, and it stood naked,
and nothing remained but aggression, We repaid them as they had repaid."

That is: We recompensed them for their doing, as they did, by way of mushakala (reciprocal matching), or as they had recompensed before, if their transgression arose from vengeance as well. This is the meaning specified here, although "al-din" has many usages in Arabic speech.

Know that the attribute of Him, exalted, as "Malik of the Day of Judgement" completes the bringing together of all the attributes of greatness and perfection upon His name, for after He was described as "Lord of the worlds", which is the meaning of true divinity, surpassing what they used to describe their gods with, such as their saying "the god of the family of so-and-so". Nations used to take special gods for themselves, as God related about some of them who said ﴿This is your god and the god of Moses﴾ [Taha: 88], and He said ﴿They said: O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. Some Arab tribes had special gods; Thaqif worshipped al-Lat. The poet said:

"And Thaqif was devoted to its Lat."

And in the hadith of 'A'isha in the Muwatta': "The Ansar, before they embraced Islam, used to make the talbiya (pilgrim's call) for Manat the idol, which they worshipped at al-Mushallal" – the hadith.

So the description of God, may He be exalted, as "Lord of all the worlds", then He followed it with the two attributes "al-Rahman al-Rahim" to indicate the greatness

[Page 177]

of His mercy. Then He was described as "Malik of the Day of Judgement", which is a description with what is greater than what came before, because it announces the generality of disposal over the created beings on the Day of Recompense, which is the first of the days of eternity. So the king of that time is the possessor of the kingship from which nothing deviates from entering under His dominion, and He is the one whose kingship does not end and does not cease. Where is this attribute from the attributes of exaggeration which people bestow upon the greatest kings, such as "King of kings, Shahanshah", "King of the age", "King of the world, Shah Jahan", and what resembles that?

Together with what is in defining that day by its addition to "the din", that is the recompense, there is the inclusion of an alerting to the non-judgement of God, because the choice of the word "din", meaning recompense, is to indicate that it is the treatment of the doer with what equals his deeds for which he is recompensed, in good and evil, and that is the particular justice. God, exalted, said ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned; there is no injustice today﴾ [Ghafir: 17]. For this reason He did not say "Malik of the Day of Reckoning". So describing Him as "Malik of the Day of pure justice" is a description of Him with the most noble meaning of kingship, for kings' praises become perpetual according to the measure of their excellence in establishing justice, and the Arabs recognised praise by that. Al-Nabigha said praising the king 'Amr ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani, king of Syria:

"How often have they repaid us with hands that are not unjust,
favour for favour, and denial for denial."

And al-Harith ibn Hilliza said praising the king 'Amr ibn Hind al-Lakhmi, king of al-Hira:

"A king who is equitable, and the best of whom are the judges,
and beneath what he possesses is the judgement."

The bringing of these sublime attributes upon His name, may He be exalted, is an allusion that the one so described deserves complete praise, which the sentence "al-hamdu lillah" (all praise is for God) expresses, because restricting the meaning of a statement to attributes of its subject indicates a relation between those attributes and the meaning of the statement, a relation understood from the context, like the explanation in the context of this verse.

Surah 1, verse 5 (part 1 of 3)

﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.﴾ When the one praising has completed his praise of his Lord, he begins to turn toward Him by manifesting sincerity to Him. This is a transition from expressing the rights of the Lord to showing attention to what His right requires of His servant, namely singling Him out in worship and in seeking help. Therefore this statement is a fresh, initiating utterance (istie'naf ibtida'i).

Opening a discourse with glorification of the great when turning toward them, before they are addressed, is an Arabic practice.

It is narrated by Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani, from Hassan ibn Thabit, who said: "I was with al-Nu'man, keeping him company and eating with him. While I was with him in a tent, a man was chanting verses around it:

Is the lord of the tent deaf, or does he hear?
O you who give the most of the camels' hard-backed ones,
Striking with the cattle-goad the flies,
Having a sheath of cattle-hide on her hands,
Upon a well-trodden path, as if it were a tumult of carrion..."

Al-Nu'man said: "Is it not Abu Umama?" (the kunya of al-Nabigha). They said: "Yes." He said: "Then give him permission," and he entered.

The shift from the manner of narrative, in the third person, beginning with the words "Al-hamdu lillah" up to "Malik yawm al-din" [Al-Fatihah: 4], to the manner of direct address, beginning with "Iyyaka na'budu" up to the end of the surah, is a wonderful art among the arts of eloquent speech in Arabic. In the science of Arabic literature and rhetoric it is called iltifat (a turning, a shift of grammatical person).

Concerning the definition of the technique of iltifat, there are two opinions among the authorities of rhetoric. The first is the opinion of all the authorities of rhetoric other than al-Sakkaki: that the speaker, after expressing a self by one of three means, speaking in the first person, the third person, or the second person, shifts in his speech and expresses that same self by another of these three means. Al-Sakkaki differed from them and defined iltifat as expressing a self by one of the means of speech in the first person, the second person, or the third person, deviating from the one that was the most appropriate for expression in that speech to another of them.

The effect of the difference between the majority and al-Sakkaki appears in the embellishment called tajrid (abstraction, in the science of badi', rhetorical ornamentation), such as the words of 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah at the beginning of his qasidah:

"Your heart was moved by the beautiful women, and it is restless..."

Here he addresses his own soul in the manner of tajrid. According to the majority this is not iltifat, but according to al-Sakkaki it is counted as iltifat. The naming of this as iltifat according to the majority's view is based on the consideration that the speaker's deviation from the path he was following to another path resembles the state of one who looks at something and then turns away from it. As for its naming as iltifat according to al-Sakkaki's view, it follows the consideration of the most common forms of iltifat, excluding the form of tajrid. Perhaps al-Sakkaki adopted this naming because it had become established before him, so he followed the majority in this term.

[p. 179]

What must be noted is that the apparent noun is regarded as belonging to the category of the third person according to both opinions. Therefore the words of the Exalted, "Iyyaka na'budu," constitute an iltifat according to both opinions, because what preceded from the beginning of the surah up to "Iyyaka na'budu" is expression by an apparent noun, namely the Name of Majesty (Allah) and His attributes.

The people of rhetoric take care with iltifat because in it there is a renewal of the style of expressing the same meaning, to avoid repeating a single style many times. Through renewing the style, the listener's attentiveness is renewed, so that he does not become bored by the repetition of one particular style.

Al-Sakkaki said in al-Miftah, after mentioning that the Arabs use iltifat frequently: "Do they then excel in hospitality to bodies, varying between one flavour and another, yet not excel in hospitality to souls, varying between one style and another? This is a consistent benefit of iltifat. Moreover, eloquent people do not generally confine themselves to it, but observe in iltifat subtle points and appropriate relations, and the people of criticism and literature have not ceased to extract these from their depths."

What is here is a wonderful iltifat. When the one praising praised God, the Exalted, and described Him with the greatest attributes, his thought reached its limit. He imagined himself in the presence of Lordship, so he addressed his Lord with attention. This is the reverse of this iltifat, in the words of Muhammad ibn Bashir al-Kharijī, of the Banu Kharijah, a tribe:

"You were blamed and not praised, and I have encountered a need
whose reward and favour someone other than you has taken.
A lowly opinion refused you the acquisition of praise,
and a soul whose God has made poor in goodness has sold it.
When it urges you toward good once,
it disobeys you; and if it intends evil, it obeys it."

He addressed him at first, then mentioned the deficiency of his opinion and the failure of his soul to be impressed by goodness. So he shifted from addressing him to expressing him by the pronoun of the third person, saying "When it urges you," as if he had imagined him diminished until he was absent from him.

The opposite of this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and in meeting Him, those have despaired of My mercy﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 23]. This is because of the consideration of vilifying the disbelief of those spoken about, in that they disbelieved in the signs of the Possessor of that majestic Name. After establishing that, he moved to the style of the first-person pronoun, since that is the original form of expression for things attributed to the speaker's own self.

What adds to the impact of the iltifat in the verse is that it moves from praise to supplication. Without doubt supplication requires direct address. So the words "Iyyaka na'budu" were a transition to what follows: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. A parallel to this is the words of al-Nabigha in lamenting al-Nu'man al-Ghassani:

"My heedlessness refused, for when I remember him
a disease stirs within my heart, the inner one.

[p. 180]

My inherited wealth, when I look upon it, and my armour,
and my mare, and what the fingers have gathered...
Your gift, and the noble she-camels, as if they were
white camels of the wild-cattle type, upon which saddles are carried."

Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni calls iltifat "the bravery of Arabic," as if he meant that it is evidence of the sharpness of the eloquent person's mind and his capacity to manipulate the styles of his speech as he wills, just as a brave warrior manoeuvres on the battlefield with advance and retreat.

"Iyyaka" is a second-person pronoun in the accusative case. The more apparent view is that the word "iyya" was made so that the pronoun could lean on it when it is detached, and for this reason pronominal suffixes attach to it, as in: "Iyyaya ta'ni" (it is me you mean), "Iyyaka a'ni" (it is you I mean), "Iyyahum arju" (it is them I hope for). From this, it is obligatory in the case of warning, because the pronoun is detached when the verb is obligatorily omitted.

Some grammarians consider "iyya" to be a separate pronoun that is fixed in one form, and that the pronouns attached to it are added for emphasis. Others consider "iyya" to be the pronoun itself, and what follows it to be particles explaining the pronoun. Others consider "iyya" to be a support for the pronoun, just as "ayy" is a support for the vocative noun with the definite article "al-". Others consider "iyya" to be an apparent noun, made genitive by the pronouns.

Worship ('ibadah) is an act that indicates submission or veneration that exceeds what is customary among people. Its application to obedience is metaphorical.

In the sharia, worship is more specific. It is defined as doing what pleases the Lord of submission, compliance and avoidance; or it is the act of a responsible person contrary to the desire of his own soul, out of veneration for his Lord. Al-Razi, in his commentary on the words of the Exalted, ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], said: "Worship is the veneration of God's command and compassion toward creation."

This is the meaning on which the sharia agrees, though they differ in form, quantity and number. Thus by this explanation it includes complying with all the rulings of the Sharia.

The Sufis have explained worship as doing what pleases the Lord. Servitude ('ubudiyyah) is contentment with what the Lord does. So it is stronger. Some of them said: "Servitude is fulfilling covenants, guarding limits, contentment with what exists, and patience with what is lost." These are terminologies about which there is no dispute.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: "The levels of worship are three. The first is that one worships God out of desire for reward and fear of punishment; this is worship, and it is a low and fallen rank, because he made the Truth a means to obtain the sought-after object.

The second is that one worships God in order to be honoured by worshipping Him and by being associated with Him through accepting His obligations. This is higher than the first, except that it is not complete, because what is intended in essence is other than God.

The third is that one worships God because He is a God, the Creator, deserving of worship, and because he himself is a servant of Him. This is the highest station, and it is what is named servitude." End of quotation.

I say: The Imam did not name the third level with a name, and it is apparent that it is connected in name with the third level, namely servitude, because Ibn Sina said in al-Isharat: "The knower wants the Truth for nothing other than Himself, and prefers nothing over his knowledge of Him, and his worship of Him is solely for Him, because He deserves worship, and because it is a noble relation to Him, not out of desire or fear." End of quotation. So he made the two one state.

What al-Fakhr claimed about the fall of the first level and the lowering of its rank is dominated by the terminology of extreme Sufis. Otherwise, worship out of hope and fear is what Islam called for in all its guidance, and it is what the majority of believers practise, and it is the goal of obligation. How could it not be, when the Exalted said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]? If the responsible person reaches the other two levels, that is a great virtue, and those who attain it are few. Moreover, one is not free from considering fear and hope in many states. Yes, the distinguished people of the community differ in their need for being made to fear and being given hope, in proportion to their differences in knowledge of the secrets of obligation and its benefits, and their differences in their ability to overcome their souls. Despite that, they have no escape from returning to fear in many states and to hope in many more.

The greatest evidence for what we have said is that Allah, the Exalted, praised the God-fearing in His Book in many places and called to taqwa (God-consciousness). Is taqwa anything other than, by its name, fear and guarding oneself against the wrath of Allah? The Exalted said: ﴿They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment; indeed the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared﴾ [al-Isra': 57].

The third level is what the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to, when someone said to him: "How do you exert yourself in worship when Allah has forgiven you your earlier and later sins?" He said: "Shall I not be a grateful servant?" Because it is apparent that gratitude here is for a blessing already received, there is no share in it for the soul through hope for more, since the general forgiveness had already been granted to him. So gratitude became for the sake of the One being thanked alone, and it was purely that it was neither out of fear nor hope.

[p. 182]

Know that among the most important investigations is the inquiry into the secret of worship, its effect, and the secret of its being prescribed for us. That is because Allah, the Exalted, created this world to be a manifestation of the perfection of His attributes, the Exalted: existence, knowledge, and power. He made man's receptivity to perfections, by the measure of which one knows the proportion of the extent of his knowledge and power relative to the knowledge and power of Allah, the Exalted. He endowed him with the spirit and the intellect, by which the ascent toward perfection increases, so that he would not be content with what he has reached of the levels at the peak of perfection and knowledge. He guided him and directed him to what he may seek help with to attain his aim, so that through swift ascent there would be for him an elevation to come that does not perish. He made his readiness to accept all goods, both immediate and deferred, dependent on instruction from the noble scribes who were given revelation of the foundations of virtues.

[p. 183]

When this depended on self-monitoring (muraqabat al-nafs) against its impulses and lapses, and that monitoring requires remembering the One who rewards good and its opposite, worship was prescribed as a reminder of that Rewarder. This is because the absence of His presence, and His being veiled by the veils of majesty, causes forgetfulness of Him to seep into souls. Likewise, since He made His order in this world closely interconnected among its members, He commanded them to observe the manners of living together and of dealing with one another, so that the order would not be corrupted. And for the constant monitoring of this as well, worship was prescribed to remind them of it. Moreover, in that remembrance there is a continuous reflection on the Creator and His affairs, and in that there is a gradual adornment with perfections. It thus becomes clear that worship is the path to perfection, both individual and social, in its beginning and its end. With this the meaning of His saying, ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], becomes clear. Worship, in general, is nothing other than that which realizes the purpose of creation. Since the secret of creation and its ultimate aim are beyond full comprehension, God Most High made us know them through their manifestation and what realizes them, gathering great meanings into a single sentence, which is the sentence ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾.

Close to this explanation which we have outlined, and less than it, is the statement of Shaykh Ibn Sina in al-Isharat: "When a human being is not such that he can stand alone in managing his own affairs except through the partnership of another from his own kind, and through exchange and counter-exchange occurring between them, each of them frees the other from an important matter which, if he undertook it by himself, many would crowd around the one person, and it would be difficult, if possible at all. Therefore, there must be among people a dealing and justice, preserved by a law imposed by a lawgiver distinguished by the right to be obeyed. And it must be that the good-doer and the wrongdoer have a recompense from the Mighty, the All-Aware. Thus it became necessary to know the Rewarder and the Lawgiver, and that together with the knowledge there be a preserving cause for that knowledge. So worship was imposed upon them, reminding them of the One worshipped, and it was repeated for them so that the reminding would be preserved through repetition." End of quotation.

There is no doubt that the motive for worship is glorification and reverence, and it is either from love or from pure fear. The most important of these is what comes from love, because it pleases the soul of the one who performs it. He said:

"I revere you out of reverence, though you have no power over me,
but a beloved whom the eye is filled with."

This [love] entails fear of the anger of the beloved. Mahmud al-Warraq, or Mansur al-Faqih, said:

"You disobey God while you display His love;
by my life, this is a wondrous thing in analogy.
If your love were sincere, you would obey Him,
for the lover is obedient to the one he loves."

For this reason God Most High said: ﴿Say: If you love God, then follow me; God will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31]. This indicates that following the Law necessitates God's love, and that the lover wishes that his Beloved should love him, as al-Mutanabbi said:

"You are the beloved, but I seek refuge in Him
from being a lover who is not loved."

To this type return the worship of most nations, including the worship prescribed in all the laws, because it is founded upon love of God Most High. Likewise is the worship of the polytheists for their idols. God Most High said: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides God, equals, whom they love as they love God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. Among the nations are those who worshipped out of fear without love, and it is only to avoid evil, as some nations worshipped the devils. The Manichaeans among the Magians worshipped the deity Ahriman, who in their view is the lord of evil and harm, and they symbolize him by the element of darkness, and claim that he was generated from an evil thought that occurred to the Lord Yazdan, the god of good. Al-Ma'arri said:

"Yazdan thought in a moment of heedlessness,
and from his thinking Ahriman was fashioned."

The restriction (hasr) derived from the fronting of the object in God's saying, "﴿You alone we worship﴾" is a true restriction, because the believers taught this praise do not worship anyone except God.

Ibn al-Hajib, in his Idah al-Mufassal in explaining the preface of al-Mufassal at Zamakhshari's words "God is most praiseworthy", claimed that fronting only conveys emphasis (ihtimam) and not restriction, and that God's saying "﴿You alone we worship﴾" is the fronting of the object for emphasis, not for qasr, and that their reliance on His saying "﴿Rather, worship God alone﴾" [al-Zumar: 66] is weak, because of the occurrence of "﴿So worship God, making religion sincerely His﴾" [al-Zumar: 2]. The refutation of his opinion is established in the books of the science of ma'ani (rhetoric). I see that his reasoning from the occurrence of His saying "﴿So worship God﴾" [al-Zumar: 2] is unbecoming to his scholarly standing, since it is not to be supposed that the meanings of speech are identical in every context.

"﴿And You alone we ask for help﴾" is a sentence conjoined to the sentence "﴿You alone we worship﴾". It was not separated from the sentence "﴿You alone we worship﴾" by the method of enumerating sentences, which is used in contexts of supplication and similar contexts of enumeration and repetition, wholly or partly, but to indicate that both acts occur together in the intention of the speakers with this specification, meaning: we single You out for help as well, together with singling You out for worship.

Istina'ah (seeking help) is asking for aid. 'Awn (aid) and i'anah (assistance) mean facilitating the performance of something that is difficult and burdensome for the one seeking help alone. It is achieved by preparing the means of accomplishing it, through lending a tool, or through participation by bodily labor, such as carrying or leading, or by speech, such as guidance and teaching, or by opinion, such as advice. Al-Hariri said in the maqama: "And a moral (aid), what an excellent help," or by wealth, such as paying a debt, such that the matter is achieved with hardship through the efforts of both the one seeking help and the one helping.

As for seeking help from God, it is asking for assistance in what no human has the capacity to achieve with help, and what the one seeking help cannot accomplish by himself alone. For this reason it indicates that the one seeking help expends his own capacity to accomplish the act and asks God for help in it, by facilitating what is beyond the capacity of the one seeking help to accomplish alone. This is the assistance in the legal sense. The scholars have explained it as the creation of what completes the act or makes it easier. It is divided into two parts: the necessary (darurriyyah), meaning what the act depends upon, so that it does not occur without it, that is, it does not occur without the presence of its requirements, namely: granting the doer capability, conceiving the act, and the availability of the material and the instrument. The totality of these four is expressed by istita'ah (ability), and it is also expressed by the soundness of the causes and instruments, and by it the obligation of the one who is able is valid.

The second part is non-necessary assistance, which should be specifically called i'anah (help): the helper's provision of what makes the act easy for the one being helped, so that it becomes simple for him and near to him, like preparing a mount for travel for one who is capable of walking. By combining this meaning with the first meaning, the reality of tawfiq (divine enabling), defined by them as God's creation of the capability and the motive toward obedience, is completed. Al-Raghib named this second part tawfiq. There is no contradiction between his statement and their definition, since, as you know, it does not occur except after the occurrence of assistance in the first sense, so tawfiq is complete.

The intended meaning here is seeking help in all important acts, the highest of which is receiving the religion, and everything whose subduing is difficult for a person, such as turning souls toward good, and what follows from that of acquiring virtues.

The indication of this intended meaning is its being written at the opening of the Book, and the specification of help occurring right after the specification of worship. For this reason, the object of "nasta'in" (we seek help), which ought to be mentioned in the genitive with "ala" (upon), was omitted. This important omission has conveyed the generality of the seeking of help, restricted to asking from God, out of courtesy toward Him Most High, and what follows from it and its causes, namely knowledges, guidance, laws, and the foundations of sciences. All of these are part of the help sought, and all of them are from God Most High. He is the One who inspired us with the principles of sciences, imposed the laws upon us, and taught us speech. He said: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes﴾ [al-Balad: 8], ﴿and a tongue and two lips﴾ [al-Balad: 9], ﴿and guided him to the two paths﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. The first is an allusion to the path of knowledge, whose root is the sensibles and whose highest is what is seen. The second is an allusion to speech and clarification for teaching, and the third is to the laws.

[p. 185]

The restriction derived from the fronting in His saying "and You alone we ask for help" is an claimed restriction (hasr idda'i) for the sake of exaggeration, because the ordinary forms of help among people, in their affairs with one another, are not counted. The meaning of the restriction here is: we do not seek help in great matters in which people cannot be helped except by God Most High.

This restriction in both clauses conveys an allusive reference (ta'ridh) to the polytheists who worship other than God and seek help from other than Him, because they were two groups. Among them were those who worshipped other than God with the intention of associating partners with Him, but their passion and infatuation with other than God made them forget the worship of God Most High, as the Sabaeans worshipped the sun, the Persians worshipped light and darkness, the Copts worshipped the calf and deified the pharaohs, and the peoples of the Sudan worshipped animals such as snakes.

Among the polytheists were those who associated the worship of others with the worship of God. This is the situation of most of the Arabs who worshipped idols or worshipped the stars. Dabba, Taym, and Ukl worshipped the sun. Kinana worshipped the moon. Lakhm, Khuza'a, and some of Quraysh worshipped Sirius. Tamim worshipped Aldebaran, and Tayy worshipped the Pleiades. All of these made the deities, in their claim, a means by which they drew near to God Most High. Thus these combined worship with seeking help from them, because making them a means to God is a kind of seeking help.
