We have said that the refutation of the polytheists and the like is derived by way of allusion (ta'ridh), that is, by way of presenting the speech indirectly, because a true restriction cannot be for the refutation of belief except by allusion, since its meaning is established in reality, as al-Silkuti indicated in his gloss on the commentary.

If you say: How are we commanded not to worship except God and not to seek help except from Him, as this verse indicates, when it has been reported in the Sahih that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he taught 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, said to him: "If you ask, ask God; and if you seek help, seek help from God," and so there is no restrictive form? I say: Our grandfather, the Shaykh, may God sanctify his spirit, mentioned in his commentary on this hadith that leaving out the method of restriction indicates that the context does not admit association, and that it is fitting for asking to be directed to none but the Capable, the Knowing.

The scholars of rhetoric have said: If the act is itself restricted, using the method of restriction is superfluous speech. End of quotation.

I say, following him: The context of the hadith is not the context of the verse. The context of the hadith is a specific teaching for one who grew up, matured, and became a man in Islam, so the establishing of the restriction of the ruling is firmly settled for him, to the point of being a matter of the smallest detail. For this reason it was dispensed with. As for the context of this verse, it is the context of the opening of revelation and legislation, and the beginning of admonition and reproach. So it was appropriate to emphasize the ruling by restriction, together with an allusive reference to the state of the abominable association. Moreover, making the command with these two [worship and seeking help] as the answer to the condition (the conditional clause "if") on the occurrence of any request and any seeking of help conveys the meaning of restriction by allusion to the polytheists and disavowal of their practice, for they used to seek help from their deities. Among this is seeking the decision by arrows placed before the deities and idols.

The pronouns in "na'budu" (we worship) and "nasta'in" (we seek help) refer to the reciter of the surah together with the community of believers. In shifting from the singular pronoun to the first-person plural pronoun that includes others, there is an indication that these praises proceed from communities.

In this there is a provocation to the polytheists, since they know that the Muslims have come to power and protection. Also, it is more eloquent in praise than "a'budu" (I worship) and "asta'in" (I seek help), so that the intimate address is not devoid of praise as well, that the Praised, the Worshipped, the Sought-for has been witnessed by communities and they have recognized His virtue. Close to this is the statement of al-Nabigha in mourning al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani:

"Sitting before him are the Ghassan, hoping for his return,
and Turk, and the group of the non-Arabs, and Kabul."

For he intended, by enumerating the categories of nations, an allusion (kinaya) to the greatness of al-Nu'man and the abundance of his subjects.

Thus it is as if the one praising, when he moved from praise to intimate address (munājāt, direct conversation with God), left no opportunity from which he might seize commendation without seizing it.

The reason for placing His words ﴿You alone we worship﴾ before His words ﴿You alone we ask for help﴾ is that worship (ʿibādah, devotion and servitude) is a drawing near to the Creator, Exalted be He, so it is more deserving of being placed first in intimate address.

As for seeking help (istiʿānah), it is for the benefit of the created being, to make matters easier for him. So it is fitting that the one addressing his Lord place first what comes from his own resolve and action, before what he asks for that assists him in it. Also, seeking help from God is built upon His being the one worshipped by the one who seeks help from Him. And since among the things for which help is sought is worship itself, worship was prior to seeking help in the order of the mind.

This placement also achieved the fulfilment of the right of the surah's verse-endings (fawāṣil), which are built on a quiescent letter that is identical or close in place of articulation on the tongue. The pronoun ﴿iyyāka﴾ was repeated in the second clause, instead of conjoining the verb ﴿nasta'īn﴾ to ﴿na'budu﴾, even though both are intended together, as the conjunction of one sentence to another indicates. This is because there is a difference between the two restrictions (ḥaṣr and qaṣr, forms of exclusive limitation). The restriction in ﴿iyyāka na'budu﴾ is real (ḥaqīqī), whereas the restriction in ﴿iyyāka nasta'īn﴾ is claimed (idiʿāʾī), for the Muslim may indeed seek help from other than God, Exalted. How could he not, when God, Exalted, says ﴿Help one another in righteousness and piety﴾ [al-Mā'idah 5:2]? Yet he does not seek help in great matters except from God, and he does not regard seeking help in the true sense as anything but seeking help from God, Exalted.

[Page 187]

﴿Guide us to the straight path.﴾ Once the petitioners had praised God and described Him with attributes of majesty, they became ready to seek their noble share of guidance. They followed this with their words, ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ (al-Fatihah: 5). This is the intermediary that unites the glorification of God, the Exalted, with the manifestation of servitude, which is the servant's share in that he is a worshipper and one who seeks help, and that this is reserved for God, the Exalted. Thus this was an intermediary between praise and request. When they thought well of their Lord's turning toward them and hoped for His bounty, they came to the desire of their share and said, ﴿Guide us to the straight path.﴾ This is the share of those who seek, specifically, because it benefits them in this world and in the next. This is the interpretation appropriate to the fact that al-Fatihah stands in the position of the preface (dibajah) to the Book that was sent down as guidance and mercy for mankind. So this sentence, in relation to what precedes it, takes the position of the aim of a preface, or the subject of a sermon, or the transition (takhallus) out of a qasidah. Because the preceding sentences differ from it in being declarative and performative, this one is separated from them. This is a better interpretation than making it an answer to an implied question, as held by the author of al-Kashshaf.

Al-hidayah (guidance) is indicating the way with gentleness, and for this reason it is specified with the meaning of indicating what is good for the one indicated, because gentleness is suitable to one for whom good is intended. It is transitive to one object directly, because its meaning is the meaning of guidance-as-direction (irshad). It is transitive to the second object, the one guided, by ila (to) and by al-lam (for). Both usages are attested. You say, "I guided him to such-and-such," meaning I brought him to knowledge of it, and "I guided him to such-and-such" meaning I directed him for such-and-such, as in ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ (al-Saffat: 23), and ﴿Praise be to God who guided us to this﴾ (al-A'raf: 43). It may also be transitive to the second object directly, as here, by way of implying the meaning of 'arafa (to know). It is said this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Others do not make it transitive directly. They regard its direct transitivity as a form of extension (tawassu'), expressed by the terms hadhf (omission) and iysal (conveyance).

It is said that the difference between the transitive form and the other is that the transitive form is used in guidance for someone who is already on the road or similar, in order that he may increase in guidance, and its verbal noun then is hidayah. As for hadahu ila kadha or li-kadha, it is used for someone who has not yet been travelling on the road, and its verbal noun is hudan. It seems the proponent of this view considered that the transitive form with a particle is so transitive for the purpose of strengthening it. The strengthening is either intended to strengthen the governing verb because of its weakness in acting through being secondary or delayed, or intended to strengthen its meaning. The truth is that this distinction, if established, is a predominant tendency, and it is a specification of usage. It does not require that the verb's meanings differ according to the manner of its transitivity, because a verb's meanings do not differ in regard to how it is made transitive unless it is implicitly given the meaning of another verb.

[Page 188]

Moreover, both hudan and hidayah are verbal nouns of the form ism masdar, and the masdar is hady. What I hold is that transitivity and intransitivity are not among the things that are fashioned by hand or agreed upon by someone. Rather, they follow from the meaning of the event signified by the verb. If the event's meaning is complete through merely conceiving the one who performs it, then it is an intransitive verb (fi'l qasir). If it is not complete except through conceiving the one who performs it and the one upon whom it falls, then it is transitive to one or more objects. If verbs become ambiguous, their ambiguity arises from the lack of clarity in the specific event intended, because their meaning revolves around several meanings.

"Hada" is certainly transitive to one object. The discussion concerns its transitivity to a second. The truth is that if the meaning of manifestation and clarification (al-irada wa-l-ibanah) is taken into account in it, it is transitive directly. If mere general guidance and indication is taken into account, it is transitive by means of a particle. Thus the mode of its transitivity indicates the event it includes.

It has been said that the reality of hidayah is indicating the road to reach the intended place. So the guide (hadi) is one who knows the routes. In the hadith of the Hijrah: "Abu Bakr hired a man from the Banu al-Dil as a guide, an expert (khirrit)." The various meanings arising from hidayah are figurative usages that have become common. The term hidayah in religious terminology, when attributed to God, the Exalted, means indicating what pleases God in doing good, and its opposite is misguidance (dalalah), which is deception (taghrir).

The scholars of kalam differed over whether the condition of conveying one to good is part of the reality of hidayah. The majority hold that it is not, and that hidayah is indicating the road of arrival, whether or not arrival takes place. This is the view of the Ash'ariyyah (followers of al-Ash'ari), and it is the correct view. Al-Zamakhshari and a group of others held that hidayah is indicating together with conveying, otherwise it would not be distinguished from misguidance, since God is capable of conveying the one He guides to what He guided him to. The root of this disagreement returns to their differing over another principle, namely the meaning of God's pleasure, will, volition and command. The followers of al-Ash'ari took into account the guidance that falls under the command. The Mu'tazilah considered the guidance that falls under the creative determination and creation. There is no disagreement that guidance together with arrival is what is legally required from both the guide and the one guided, even though error may occur on the part of the guide and poor acceptance on the part of the one guided. This is the meaning of what 'Abd al-Hakim chose: that the term is laid down in the Shari'ah for the common element, because it occurs in the Qur'an in both senses. He said, ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ (al-Qasas: 56), and He said, ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ (Fussilat: 17). The default assumption is that the term is not homonymous and not figurative.

Guidance has types that fall under four ordered classes. The first is granting the motive and perceptive faculties by which the human being is guided to the coherence of his existence as a person. This includes types that begin with the infant's inspired suckling of the breast and crying at pain, and reach to the emotional faculties by which he repels from himself what harms him, such as perceiving the terror of destructive things and the ugliness of repugnant things, and by which he secures his existential interests, such as seeking food and water, warding insects away from himself, scratching the skin, and the eyelid twitching when something harmful passes before it. Its culmination is the states of thought, which is the movement of the soul among intelligibles, that is, considering the intelligible in order to obtain the unknown from the self-evident. This is the rational faculty that is peculiar to the human being, abstracted from sensible knowledge.

The second is establishing proofs that distinguish truth from falsehood and correct from wrong. This is the guidance of theoretical sciences. The third is guidance to what the proofs may fall short of reaching, or whose application to such matters would lead to hardship. This comes through sending messengers and sending down books and balances of justice. To this the Qur'an refers in His words concerning the messengers: ﴿And We made them leaders who guide by Our command﴾ (al-Anbiya': 73). The fourth, the highest class of guidance, is the unveiling of supreme realities and the manifestation of the secrets of meanings in which the minds of the wise are bewildered, either through revelation and sound inspiration or through divine manifestations. God, the Exalted, has named this guidance when He attributed it to the prophets, saying, ﴿Those are the ones God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ (al-An'am: 90). There is no doubt that what is sought by the words "Guide us" (ihdina), taught to the believers, is what suits the state of the one who supplicates with it, if taken as the supplication of a particular individual or particular group when they say "Guide us." Or it is the types of guidance in general, considering their distribution among those who are qualified for them according to their capacity, if it is a supplication upon the tongue of all the believers addressed by the Qur'an. In both cases, some types of guidance are sought to be attained by one who has not yet reached them, and some are sought to be continued for one who already has them, either specifically or for all people who have them. This is like the guidance we have before we ask for it, similar to the majority of the types of the first class.

The form of the imperative is laid down for seeking the attainment of the required reality, whether an act or a restraint. When it is used to seek continuation, its use is figurative, as in ﴿O you who believe, believe﴾ (al-Nisa': 136), where only the seeking of continuation is intended.

As for when it is used to seek continuation together with increase of what has partly been attained and partly not, then it is used in its literal meaning, which is seeking attainment, because increase in the levels of guidance, for example, is the attainment of further materials from it.

Since seeking increase necessarily entails seeking the continuation of what has been attained, since increase hardly benefits if the foundation is broken, its use in that case is in its necessary meaning alongside its primary meaning. So it is a kinayah (metonymy). But when the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who has reached all levels of guidance and ascended to the summit of its ends, says, ﴿Guide us to the straight path,﴾ his supplication in that case is a use of the word in the figurative sense of its meaning, and his supplication is then an iqtibas (allusive borrowing) from the verse, and it is not the exact intended meaning of the verse, because what is intended by the verse is seeking attainment through increase together with seeking continuation by way of implication. There is no doubt that the intended meaning in the verse is seeking perfect guidance.

Al-sirat means the road. It is pronounced with sad and with sin, and both are read in the well-known readings. Most Arabs pronounce it with sin, except the people of the Hijaz, who pronounce it with sad, changed from sin, for the sake of lightness in moving from sin to ra' and then to ta'. Al-Ja'bari, quoted in Lata'if al-Isharat, said that they do this with every sin followed by ghayn, kha', qaf or ta', and they changed it to sad here so that it would match ta' in emphasis, elevation and heaviness, together with ra', to avoid the difficulty of moving from a low place to a high one, end quote. That is, in contrast to the reverse, as in tast (basin), because the first is an action and the second is an abandonment. The Qays tribe changed sin to a sound between sad and zay, which is ishmam (a partial, colored pronunciation), and Hamzah read it this way in Khalaf's transmission from him. Some Arabs changed sin into pure zay. Al-Qurtubi said this is the dialect of 'Udhrah, Kalb and Banu al-Qayn, and it is inferior and was not used in recitation. The recitation with sad is the one of the eloquent standard language, and most readers recite with sad. Ibn Kathir in Qunbul's transmission recites with sin. The recitation with sad is the preferred one, because it agrees with the orthography of the Mushaf and is the eloquent standard language.

If it is asked: how was it written in the Mushaf with sad when some readers recited it with sin? I say: the Companions wrote it with sad to draw attention to the more eloquent form, because they wrote in the dialect of Quraysh and relied on the knowledge of the Arabs. Those who recited with sin interpreted that the Companions did not abandon the sin pronunciation because they knew it, so they gave equal weight to the more eloquent form and the original form. If they had written it with sin, though that is the original, people would have supposed it was not permissible to deviate from it, because it is the original and the written form, just as they wrote al-musaytir with sad, even though its original is with sin. This is a case where the disagreement goes back to a difference in the pronunciation of the word and not to the root of the word, because of the well-known variation of tribal dialects in a word while its form is one among them.

Al-sirat is an Arabic noun. No lexicographer has said it is an arabicized word. But al-Naqqash and Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned in al-Itqan that it means the road in the language of the Romans. It is mentioned that Abu Hatim mentioned this in his book al-Zinah, and al-Suyuti built on this and included it in his versified work on arabicized words. In this verse, al-sirat is used metaphorically for the meaning of the truth by which its seeker reaches the attainment of God's pleasure, because that attainment is what Islam came to seek.

[Page 191]

Al-mustaqim is the active participle of istaqama, the reflexive of qawwamtuhu, so that istaqama. Al-mustaqim is that which has no crookedness in it and no curves. The best of roads is the one that is straight, which is the main road, because by its straightness it is closer to the intended place than others, so its traveller does not go astray in it, nor wander, nor become confused.

The straight path (al-mustaqim) is used here as a metaphor for the clear truth that is not mixed with any doubt of falsehood. It is like a road with no side-paths branching off it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "the straight path is the religion of truth," and it is also narrated from him that it is "the religion of Islam." His statements explain one another. He does not mean that they were taught to ask for guidance to a religion that had already passed away, although all the divine religions were straight paths according to the circumstances of their respective communities. This is confirmed by the words of God, Exalted, in relating the seduction of Satan: ﴿He said, "Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path."﴾ [al-A'raf: 16] [111]

The definiteness in "al-sirat al-mustaqim" is definiteness by mental reference (ta'rif al-'ahd al-dhihni), because they asked for guidance to this category as it is embodied in one individual, namely the one exclusively characterized by uprightness. This is because uprightness does not have multiple forms, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus: 32]. Error, however, has many kinds, as He said: ﴿Even if the abundance of the evil impresses you.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100]

This interpretation may also be understood as referring to the attainment of guidance to Islam: God taught them this supplication to show His favour, and God had already guided them through what preceded in the Qur'an before the revelation of al-Fatihah, and He guides them through what follows of the Qur'an and the Prophetic guidance (al-irshad al-nabawi).

The application of "the straight path" to the religion of Islam occurs in His words: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion."﴾ [al-An'am: 161].

In my view, the more apparent meaning is that the straight path refers to all righteous knowledge and deeds, both belief and action, by which God enables them to reach the truth and to distinguish it from error, according to the measure of the readiness of souls and the breadth of the field of bright intellects, and to righteous actions, such that deviation and doubts do not afflict them in their religion. This is more appropriate, so that the supplication is a request for the attainment of what is not yet attained at the time of asking. Indeed, a person needs this guidance in all his affairs, even in persisting in the good he is already engaged in, to protect himself from falling short in it or from deviating from it.

Guidance to Islam is not restricted to the beginning of following and adopting it; rather, it is continuous with the continuity of its legislation and rulings, whether by explicit text or by deduction. And by this the position of His words becomes clear: ﴿not of those who have evoked anger or of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], hitting the target (musadifan al-mihazz).

[Page 192]

**"The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour"** (*ṣirāṭa alladhīna an‘amta ‘alayhim*) is a substitute (*badal*) or an explicative apposition (*‘aṭf bayān*, an apposition that clarifies the noun it follows) for "the straight path" (*al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*). The verse was arranged in the form of substitution or explication, rather than saying "Guide us to the straight path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour," for two benefits.

The first: the primary aim of the request is that the path to which one is guided be clearly a means of salvation, gentle, and easy. That it is the way of those whom God has favoured is an additional matter, serving to show His grace.

The second benefit is what the form of substitution contains of summary followed by detail, so that the meaning of "the path," as the object of the request, takes firmer hold in the souls of the believers who were taught this supplication. It therefore has the same benefit as moral emphasis (*al-tawkīd al-ma‘nawī*). Also, in this form there is an affirmation of the reality of this path and a confirmation of its concept in their souls, so that its concept is realised twice. It thus gains the benefit achieved by verbal emphasis (*al-tawkīd al-lafẓī*). Considering it a substitution is equal to considering it an explicative apposition; neither has any superiority over the other, contrary to those who attempted to prefer one over the other. For in my view the truth is that explicative apposition is a name for a type of substitution, namely the matching substitute (*al-badal al-muṭābiq*), and none of the grammarians has made clear any semantic distinction between them, nor any evidence that determines a resort to one rather than the other.

Al-Zamakhsharī said in *al-Kashshāf*: "If you ask, what is the benefit of the substitute? I say: its benefit is emphasis, because of what it contains of repetition and reiteration." End of quotation. His words convey that the benefit of substitution is two matters, both returning to emphasis: the first is what it contains of repetition, meaning the repetition of the substitute's word and the substituted word. By "reiteration" he meant what the substitute conveys according to the grammarians, namely the repetition of the governing element (*takrīr al-‘āmil*). He had prepared for this at the start of his statement by saying: "It is in the ruling of the repetition of the governing element, as if it were said: guide us to the straight path, guide us to the path of those..." He called it reiteration because it is the repetition of the very same word. This is unlike the repetition of the word of the substituted noun, which is a restatement of it using something that coincides with its referent. For this reason he used the terms "reiteration" and "repetition." His meaning is that this kind of substitute, which involves repeating the word of the substituted noun, gives the benefit of substitution and the benefit of verbal emphasis. You know that combining the two matters cannot be achieved in a manner recognised by eloquent speakers except through this artful construction.

Repeating the noun in the substitute or the explicative apposition, so that what is intended to be connected with the first noun may be built upon it, is a delightful style of eloquent speech. Repeating the word indicates that its referent is a matter of special care and is dear to the soul. Similar to this is the repetition of the verb, as in God's words: ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ (al-Furqān 25:72), and His words: ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ 28:63). The repetition of the verb "passed by" (*marrū*) and the verb "led them astray" (*aghwaynāhum*), with the complement attached to the repeated verb rather than to the first verb without repetition, carries a splendour and delight that you would not find if it were attached to the first verb without repetition. The repetition in such a case is not merely for emphasis, because something has been added to it that is connected with it.

Ibn Jinnī said in his commentary on the difficult passages of *al-Ḥamāsa*, regarding the verse of al-Aḥwaṣ:

*fa-idhā tazūlu tazūlu ‘an mutakhammiṭin / tukhsha bawādiruhu ‘alā al-aqrān*

("When he moves, he moves away from a raging lion whose sudden attacks on his rivals are feared.")

"It would be impossible to say: if I stand, I stand, and if I sit, I sit, because in the second there is nothing other than what is in the first. But the poet could say 'when he moves, he moves' because of the preposition that is attached to the second verb, from which the benefit is derived. Similar to this is God's words: ﴿These are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ 28:63). Abū ‘Alī, meaning al-Fārisī, had refrained in this verse from what we have taken." End of quotation.

I say: The reason for Abū ‘Alī's refraining is not clear. Perhaps he refrained from regarding "we led them astray" (*aghwaynāhum*) as a substitute for "we led astray" (*aghwaynā*), and made it a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*), even though the outcome is one. In mentioning those upon whom God has bestowed favour by means of the relative pronoun, and in attributing the act of bestowing favour to them to the pronoun of majesty (God), there is an honouring of their status, in contrast to others: those who earned anger and those who went astray.

Furthermore, in choosing to describe the straight path as "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour," rather than any of its other attributes, there is a preparation for a welcoming of the request. For when you say to a generous person, "Give me as You gave so-and-so," this is more stirring to his generosity. This was affirmed by the Shaykh al-Jadd (my grandfather), may God sanctify his secret, in regard to the Prophet's words (ﷺ): "As You blessed Abraham." Thus the petitioners say: "Guide us to the straight path, the path to which You guided the servants of Your blessings." This also includes a subtle allusion to requesting that they be counted, in the rank of guidance, among those who were favoured, and an aspiration to follow them in taking the means by which they ascended to those ranks. God said: ﴿There has been for you an excellent example in them﴾ (al-Mumtaḥina 60:6). It is also a preparation for what comes afterwards regarding disassociation from the states of those who earned anger and those who went astray. Thus this contains an optimism and a seeking of refuge.

*Al-ni‘mah* (favour), whether with a kasra or a fatḥa, is derived from *al-na‘īm*, which is the ease of living, what is agreeable to a person, and comfort. Its verb is like *samiʿa*, *naṣara*, and *ḍaraba*.

*Al-ni‘mah* is a good condition, because the pattern *fi‘la* with a kasra is for states (*hay’āt*). The objects of favour are sensory pleasures, and then it is used for non-sensory pleasures that return a benefit, even if the one who possesses them does not perceive them.

Thus what is meant by favour in God's words ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ is the favour that is not mixed with anything that spoils it, and whose outcome is not evil. It includes worldly goods free from bad consequences, and the goods of the Hereafter, which are the more important. It includes worldly favours both those that are bestowed and those that are acquired, both spiritual and physical, and it includes the favours of the Hereafter.

[Page 194]

Most of the favour in this sense returns to guidance, for guidance to what is acquired in this world and to all of the Hereafter clearly involves the true reality of guidance. And because what is given in this world, though it is obtained without acquisition, still depends on guidance in using well what it was given for.

Thus what is meant by "those upon whom favour has been bestowed" is those upon whom complete favours have been poured out. There is no hiding the complete appropriateness between those who were favoured and those who were guided at that point. Therefore, in substituting "the path of those" for "the straight path," there is a wondrous meaning: guidance is a favour, and those who were favoured with complete favour have been guided to the straight path.

The ones upon whom God bestowed favour are the best of earlier nations, among the messengers and prophets, who attained complete favour. It fits that the one asked for is the path of those favoured in the past, and that it is the religion of Islam which came afterwards, in view of the fact that the straight path follows the patterns of the true revealed laws in the roots of religion and the branches of guidance and piety. So they asked for a upright religion whose straightness would be like the path of those favoured, and they were answered with the religion of Islam, which combined the straightness of the earlier religions and added to it.

Or what is meant by those favoured is the prophets and messengers, for they were in a state more perfect than that of their nations. For this reason God described many of the earlier messengers with the attribute of Islam. Jacob said to his sons: ﴿Do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ (al-Baqara 2:132). That is because God showed gentleness to the nations, and did not push them to the ultimate goal intended for people, since they were not qualified to bear it. Rather, He commanded the messengers with the most perfect states, which are His intended aim for creation in the end. Let us illustrate this with the drinking of wine: a small amount of it that does not intoxicate was permissible, and intoxication was prohibited, or was not prohibited at all. But the prophets did not partake of even a small amount of intoxicants, and this is the measure to which God guided this whole community. So whether we interpret those favoured as the prophets, or as the best of their followers, or as the earlier Muslims, the aim is guidance to a complete path. This supplication is carried, in every age, toward what suits the paths of guidance that preceded that age and that did not reach their ultimate end.

What is said about the required meaning of "guide us" (*ihdinā*) under all these interpretations is like what was said earlier, regarding whether "guide us" is a request for attainment, increase, or continuance.

The supplication is based on not regarding as significant a favour that is not pure. For God's favours upon all His servants are numerous, and the disbeliever is favoured with what is beyond dispute. But these are favours surrounded by the pains of anxiety about bad outcomes, and followed by the punishment of the Hereafter. Thus the supposed disagreement between some scholars as to whether the disbeliever is one who has been favoured is a disagreement with no benefit in it. There is no point in lengthening the discussion with the apparent proofs of both groups.

**"Not of those who earned anger, nor of those who have gone astray"** (*ghayri al-maghḍūbi ‘alayhim wa lā al-ḍāllīn*)

The word "*ghayr*" (other than) is in the genitive case by the agreement of the ten canonical readers (*al-qurrāʾ al-ʿashara*), and it is a qualifier (*ṣifa*) of "those upon whom You have bestowed favour." Or it is a substitute from it, and the qualifying and the substitution are the same in the intended meaning. In *al-Kashshāf* he first presented the aspect of substitution in order to abbreviate the discussion on it, so that it would lead to a discussion on the qualifying aspect. Thus he raises the question of how it is valid to describe a definite noun by the word "*ghayr*," which is not made definite. Otherwise, making "*ghayr al-maghḍūb*" a qualifier of "those" is the correct view. Sībawayh also parsed it this way, as transmitted by Abū Ḥayyān, and he explained it by saying that substitution by an attribute is weak, since the rule is that the substitute is the very same as the substituted noun, that is, a name of an entity belonging to it. He means that the meaning of attribution in "*ghayr*" is more prominent than the meaning of another entity that is not the previous one. This is a standing at the limits of technical expressions, to the point that the author of *al-Kashshāf* needed to interpret "*ghayr al-maghḍūb*" as "those who were safe from anger." But I do not think al-Zamakhsharī intended to interpret the word "*ghayr*"; rather, he intended to explain the meaning.

The description of a definite noun by "*ghayr*" is valid together with the statement of grammarians that "*ghayr*," because of its deep indefiniteness, is not made definite by being attached to a definite noun. That is, there is no benefit in describing with it the function of distinguishing; therefore a definite noun is not described by it, since the qualifier must be more well-known than the thing qualified. "*Ghayr*," though attached to a definite noun, is because of what its meaning includes of indefiniteness, deprived of the benefit of definiteness, since everything other than the thing attached to it is "other." What is gained from the description in your saying "I passed by Zayd, other than ‘Amr"? Therefore the attribute here is either on the basis that "those upon whom You have bestowed favour" does not mean a specific group, so that its definition by the relative clause is like the definition by the generic definite article (*al-jinsiyya*), which the scholars of rhetoric (*ʿulamāʾ al-maʿānī*) call the definite article of mental reference (*lām al-ʿahd al-dhihnī*). Thus it is in meaning like an indefinite noun, although its wording is that of a definite noun. Therefore it is defined by a similar word, both in form and meaning. "*Ghayr al-maghḍūb*" is in the form of a definite noun because it is attached to a definite noun, but in meaning it is like an indefinite noun because no specific thing is intended.

Or the attribute is on the basis of the definiteness of "*ghayr*" in such usage, because when "*ghayr*" is intended to negate the opposite of the described thing, that is, what is equal to its contradictory, it becomes definite. This is because a thing is made definite by negating its opposite, as in the expression "upon you is motion, other than stillness." So when the one who was favoured is not punished, the one punished is the one who earned anger. This is what Ibn Hishām transmitted from Ibn al-Sarrāj and al-Sīrāfī, and it is what Ibn al-Ḥājib chose in his *Amālī* regarding God's words: ﴿other than those who have a harm﴾ (al-Nisā’ 4:95). He transmitted from Sībawayh that "*ghayr*" is not made definite because it has the meaning of "different" (*al-mughāyir*), so it is like an active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*). He attached to it words like *mithl* (similar), *siwā* (besides), and *ḥasb* (sufficient), and said that it becomes definite when its attachment is intended to express permanence. It seems that the outcome of the two views is one, because when "*ghayr*" is attached…

[Page 196]

To the opposite of what it describes, which is a single opposite. That is, when something is attributed to its exact contrary, otherness (ghayriyya) is fixed for it, and it becomes a permanent attribute that does not change. The otherness of a thing relative to its contrary is always established for it. So your saying "Upon you is movement, not stillness" (ʿalayka bil-ḥaraka ghayra al-sukūn) is different from your saying "I passed by Zayd, not ʿAmr." His saying ﴿not of those who have earned anger﴾ belongs to the first type.

One of the purposes of describing ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ as ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ is seeking refuge from what befell nations upon whom God bestowed favor by guiding them to the path of good according to their time, through the call of the messengers to the truth. They adopted it, but then misunderstanding came upon them, so they altered it and did not observe it with its due observance. The disavowal is from becoming like them in: insolence toward the blessing, bad compliance, corrupt interpretation, and giving precedence to worldly desires over establishing the religion, until the anger of God Most High became due upon them. Likewise, the disavowal is from the condition of those who were guided to the straight path but did not direct their care to preserving steadfastness on it, so they became among those who are astray after guidance, having mishandled the attribute of knowledge of the blessing, so their guidance turned into error. It is apparent that the anger of God did not become due upon them before Islam, because they strayed unintentionally, so God's anger did not precede upon them in the past. The Jews are among the first group, and the Christians are among the second group, as is known from examining the history of the emergence of these two religions among them.

It does not necessarily follow that the first of the two descriptions is specific to the Jews and the second to the Christians, for among the nations there are others like them. This interpretation is the one with which the situation of supplication for guidance to the straight path is consistent. Had the intended meaning been the religion of Judaism and the religion of Christianity, the supplication would have been seeking to obtain what is already obtained, since Islam came abrogating both of them. The ones upon whom anger has come and the ones who are astray include the sects of disbelief, wickedness and disobedience. "Those upon whom anger has come" is a genus for the sects that deliberately did so and made light of the religion, either intentionally or through a very far-fetched interpretation. "Those who are astray" is a genus for the sects that erred from the religion through misunderstanding and little attentiveness. Both groups are blameworthy, because we are commanded to follow the path of truth and to exert effort in reaching it. The Jews are from the first group, and the Christians from the second.

What is reported in the transmitted reports, whose apparent meaning is the interpretation of "those upon whom anger has come" as the Jews and "those who are astray" as the Christians, is an indication that the verse contains an allusion to these two groups, upon whom these two descriptions became due, because each of them became a known example for what the allusion is aimed at. It has become clear to you from this that the conjunction of "nor those who are astray" to "not of those who have earned anger" is an ascent in seeking refuge from the evil of a bad end, because seeking refuge from the error that brought its people the anger of God does not suffice in place of seeking refuge from the error that did not reach its people those depths. This is the reason for placing "those upon whom anger has come" before "nor those who are astray," because the supplication was by requesting negation, so the progression in it is achieved by negating the weaker after negating the stronger, while observing the rhyme (fawāṣil).

The anger attached to those upon whom it has come is the anger of God. The reality of anger as known among people is a state that comes over the soul, followed by a movement of the spirit outward and its surging, so it seeks retaliation. Thus the state is a cause for seeking retaliation, and seeking retaliation is a cause for the retaliation's occurrence.

What appears to me is that the will for retaliation is not among the necessary features of the quiddity of anger, such that it never separates from it. Rather, it may be among its effects. Anger is a state of the soul that arises from the occurrence of what is not agreeable to it, so there follows from it aversion to the act that is angered at and aversion to its doer. It is accompanied by turning away from the one who is angered at, treating him with harshness, withholding kindness, and harming him. This may lead to seeking retaliation against him. The threshold at which anger is aroused in the soul varies according to the differing levels of the souls' tolerance for what is disagreeable and the differing customs in regarding its causes.

Perhaps those who made the will for retaliation necessary to anger based this on the Arabic grammatical rules. Since the reality of anger is impossible to attribute to God Most High, and attributing it to Him in its literal sense is impossible, due to the definitive proofs that establish God Most High's transcendence above essential and accidental changes, it has become obligatory upon the believer to turn the attribution of anger to God away from its literal meaning. The method of the people of knowledge and reflection in this turning is that the word is turned to metaphor by the relation of necessity, or to metonymy (kināya), by using the word to refer to a necessary consequence of its meaning. Thus what is an attribute of God from the meaning of anger is its necessary consequence, namely punishment, humiliation on the Day of Recompense, and cursing, that is, distancing from the people of religion and righteousness in this world. Or it is of the kind of allegory (tamthīl). The early generations in the first century and the middle of the second century used to refrain from interpreting these ambiguous (mutashābihāt) matters, because they saw in that refraining the benefit of occupying oneself with establishing the actions that the Law intends from people. But when speculative inquiry into knowledge arose, and the pursuit of knowing the realities of things, and people's talk about the meanings of the religion emerged in a manner not agreeable to the truth, the people of knowledge found no alternative but to expand the methods of correct interpretation in order to make the Muslim understand and to suppress the heretic. So the religion stood firm through their labor on its foundations.

The one who is sincere to Him is distinguished from his deceiver and denier. Each of them, in what they did, was upon guidance. After clarification, one never returns to generality. What they interpreted is only in terms of what is known in the language of the Arabs and understood by its people.

So God Most High's anger in general returns to His dealing with those who swerve from His guidance and disobey His commands, and retaliation follows from it. Its degrees are of which the highest is the punishment of polytheists and hypocrites with eternal abiding in the lowest abyss of the Fire. Below anger is aversion (karāha). There is a report in a hadith: "He dislikes for you gossip, asking too many questions, and wasting property." Opposite these two are pleasure (riḍā) and love (maḥabba). All of this is other than will (mashīʾa) and volition (irāda), in the sense of decree and bringing into existence. So He does not approve of disbelief for His servants: ﴿If you are grateful, He is pleased with it for you﴾ [al-Zumar: 7]; ﴿Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾ [al-Anʿām: 112]; ﴿Had your Lord willed, those on earth would all have believed, all together﴾ [Yūnus: 99]. The detailed treatment of this sentence belongs to the science of kalām.

Know that anger, according to the sages of ethics, is a source from among the three fundamental moral qualities which together are expressed by justice (ʿadāla), and these are: wisdom (ḥikma), chastity (ʿiffa), and courage (shajāʿa). Thus anger is the source of courage. However, anger is also used to refer to a psychic source for many extreme and moderate traits. They call what is in man of bestial attributes the "irascible faculty" (al-quwwa al-ghaḍabiyya), and this is the love of domination. Among its benefits is the repelling of what harms him. It has a limit of moderation and a limit of deviation. Its moderation is courage, greatness of aspiration, and firmness of heart in frightening situations. Its deviation is either by excess, which is recklessness, extreme anger over a trivial matter, arrogance, self-admiration, harshness, rancor, envy, and hardheartedness; or by deficiency, which is cowardice, weakness of soul, and smallness of aspiration. When anger is mentioned without qualification in the language, it refers to some of the deviant forms of the irascible faculty. For this reason, it is among the comprehensive words of the Prophet ﷺ: "A man said to him, 'Advise me.' He said: 'Do not become angry.' He repeated it several times, and he said: 'Do not become angry.'" Narrated by al-Tirmidhī.

It was asked of one of the kings of Persia: "By what has your kingdom endured?" He said: "Because we punish according to the measure of the sin, not according to the measure of anger."

So the anger that is forbidden is anger for the sake of the self, because from it proceed injustice and aggression. Among anger there is also a praiseworthy kind, which is anger for the protection of public interests, especially religious ones. It has been reported that the Prophet ﷺ would not become angry for himself; but when a sacred limit of God's sacred limits was violated, he became angry for God.

His saying (( ﴿nor those who are astray﴾ )) is conjoined to "those upon whom anger has come," as is evident. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: the entry of "lā" is to ward off the suspicion that "those who are astray" is conjoined to "those upon whom You have bestowed favor." This is a far-fetched explanation. The truth is that "lā" is superfluous, to emphasize the negation derived from the word "ghayr," following the Arab manner regarding what is conjoined to something within the scope of negation, as in His saying ﴿that you should say: there came to us no bringer of good tidings nor warner﴾ [al-Māʾida: 19]. This is a style in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Sayyid said in the marginalia of al-Kashshāf: so that it should not be thought that what is negated is the combined whole, which would permit the affirmation of one of them. Since "ghayr" carries the meaning of negation, the negation is repeated in what is conjoined to it. The "lā" here is not superfluous in the way it is in His saying ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 12], as some exegetes have thought, because that superfluity is verbal and semantic, since the meaning there is affirmative, whereas the "lā" here is merely verbally superfluous, and the meaning is negative.

Error (ḍalāl) is following a path other than the intended one out of mistake, whether one knows that he is doing so and seeks the path, or does not know. From this comes the expression "a lost camel" (ḍāllat al-ibil). It is the opposite of guidance (hudā). The application of the term "astray" (ḍāll) to one who errs regarding religion or knowledge is a metaphor, as here. In the language of the Law, error is the opposite of being guided, and being guided is complete faith, while error is what falls short of that. They said it has a broad range: its lowest level is abandoning the Sunnas, and its highest is disbelief.

We have explained guidance earlier as indication (dalāla) conveyed with gentleness. Thus error is the absence of that, and it is applied to its most extreme kinds: sealing, stamping, and veils (akinna).

What is meant by "those upon whom anger has come" and "those who are astray" are two genera of sects of disbelief. "Those upon whom anger has come" is a genus for the sects that deliberately did so and made light of the religion, deliberately and through a very far-fetched interpretation by which the dominance of desire is excused. These sects took crooked paths from the path laid out for them, so they deserved anger, because they erred without excuse, since what led them to error was nothing but preferring worldly portions.

"Those who are astray" is a genus for the sects who distorted the true religions, deliberately and through misunderstanding. Both groups are blameworthy and punished, because creatures are commanded to follow the path of truth, to exert effort in reaching it, and to be wary of opposing its aims. Since the mention of "those upon whom anger has come" has preceded, and it is known that anger upon them was because they swerved from the path to which they were guided, thereby depriving themselves of reaching God Most High's good pleasure through it, and since "those who are astray" have strayed from the path, there arises something like an inverted parallelism (iḥtibāk), namely that each of the two groups has obtained a share of the two descriptions. However, the attachment of each description to the group to which it is attached indicates that those described as "those who are astray" are below "those upon whom anger has come" in error. So what is intended by "those upon whom anger has come" is those angered with severe anger, because their error is atrocious.

Thus the Jews are an example of the first group, and the Christians are among the second group, as the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ in the Jāmiʿ of al-Tirmidhī, which he graded as ḥasan, indicates.

What is reported in the transmitted reports interpreting "those upon whom anger has come" as the Jews and "those who are astray" as the Christians is by way of example, through the most famous sects upon whom these two descriptions became due. The Arabs knew the Jews of Khaybar, al-Naḍīr, some inhabitants of Madina, and the Arabs of Yemen. They also knew the Christian Arabs, such as Taghlib, Kalb, and some of Quḍāʿa. All of those altered and changed, and deviated from the straight path to which God had guided them, and they scattered into the byways of paths with varying degrees of such deviation.

The Jews rebelled against their prophets and rabbis more than once, and deliberately altered the Law, so the description "those upon whom anger has come" became incumbent on them and clung to them in many verses.

The Christians went astray after the disciples (al-Hawariyyun), and they misunderstood the meaning of sanctification (al-taqdis) concerning ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. So they claimed that he was the Son of God in the literal sense. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Say, O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the limits in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before and led many astray and strayed from the right way.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 77]

In describing the path that is requested in His words ﴿Guide us to the path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6] as "the straight" (al-mustaqim), there is an indication that Islam is clear in its proof and upright in its course. Its adherents do not plunge into the abyss of misguidance, as God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Say, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion﴾ [al-An'am: 161], and He says: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. This is with variation in the degrees of attaining what God, the Exalted, intends. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever strives (ijtihad) and is correct has two rewards, and whoever strives and errs has one reward."

The explanation of the Shariah has not left openings for confusion between the disagreement that falls within the scope of Islam and the disagreement that takes its holder outside the bounds of Islam. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, you are upon the clear truth﴾ [al-Naml: 79].

The reciters differed regarding the vowel of the pronoun ha' (هاء الضمير) in His words (﴿upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾) and His words ﴿not of those who have earned (Your) anger﴾, and whatever is similar to these two from every plural pronoun and masculine and feminine dual pronoun for the third person that comes after a silent ya' (ياء ساكنة). The majority read it with a kasrah on the ha', to avoid heaviness, because the ha' is a weak barrier; so if it is given a dammah after the ya', its dammah would come after a kasrah or a silent ya', and that is heavy. This is the dialect of Qays, Tamim and Sa'd ibn Bakr. Hamzah read ʿalayhim, ilayhim and ladayhim only, with a dammah on the ha', and everything else with a kasrah on the ha', such as ilayhima and sayasihim. This is the dialect of Quraysh and the people of the Hijaz. Yaʿqub read every pronoun of this type in which there is a silent ya' before the ha' with a dammah on the ha'.

We have mentioned this here, so we will not repeat it in similar cases. It belongs to the rules of the science of Qur'anic readings (ʿilm al-qira'at) concerning the ha' of the pronoun.

They also differed concerning the vowel of the mim of the masculine third-person plural pronoun in continuous recitation (al-wasl) when it comes before a moving letter. The majority read (﴿ʿalayhim ghayri al-maghdubi ʿalayhim﴾) with a silent mim. Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far and Qalun, in one narration from him, read it with an elongated dammah: "ghayri al-maghdubi ʿalayhimu," and this is a dialect of some Arabs. On it is the verse of Labid:

*And they are its horsemen, and they are its judges.*

So he brought both dialects. Warsh read with a dammah on the mim and elongation of it when a hamzah comes after the mim, as in ﴿ghayri al-maghdubi ʿalayhim﴾ (with the hamzah following). All agreed on the silence of the mim in pausal recitation (waqf).

Surat al-Baqarah

This surah is called Surat al-Baqarah in what is related from the Prophet ﷺ and in the speech of the early generations (al-salaf). It has been reported in the Sahih that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever recites the two verses at the end of Surat al-Baqarah, they will suffice him." And in it: "From ʿĀʾishah: when the verses at the end of al-Baqarah about usury were revealed, the Messenger of God recited them, then he stood and forbade trade in wine."

The reason for its naming is that it mentions the story of the cow, which God commanded the Children of Israel to slaughter as a sign, and it describes their misunderstanding of that. This is something that this surah alone mentions. In my view, it was attributed to the story of the cow to distinguish it from the surahs that begin with the disjoined letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) alif lam mim, because they would sometimes give those disjoined letters as names for the surahs in which they occur and identify them by them, such as Ta Ha, Ya Sin, and Sad. In al-Ittiqan, from al-Mustadrak, it is reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, it is the hump (sanam) of the Qur'an." The hump of anything is its highest part. This is not a proper name for it, but it is a description of honor.

Likewise is the saying of Khalid ibn Ma'dan: "It is the tent (fustat) of the Qur'an." A fustat is that which encloses a place, because it encloses many rulings.

Surat al-Baqarah was revealed in Medina, by consensus, and it was the first to be revealed in Medina. Ibn Hajar, in his commentary on al-Bukhari, related the consensus on this. It has been said that Surat al-Mutaffifin was revealed before it, based on the view that Surat al-Mutaffifin is Medinan. There is no doubt that Surat al-Baqarah contains the obligation of fasting, and fasting was made obligatory in the first year after the Hijrah. The fasting of ʿAshura' was made obligatory in it, then the fasting of Ramadan was made obligatory in the second year, because the Prophet ﷺ fasted seven Ramadans, the first of which was the Ramadan of the second year after the Hijrah. So Surat al-Baqarah was revealed in the first year after the Hijrah, toward its end, or in the second year.

In al-Bukhari, from ʿĀʾishah: "Surat al-Baqarah was not revealed except while I was with him," meaning the Prophet ﷺ. The consummation of the marriage of the Messenger of God with ʿĀʾishah was in Shawwal of the first year after the Hijrah. It has also been said that it was at the beginning of the second year. It is narrated from her that she remained with him nine years, and when he died she was eighteen years old, and he consummated the marriage with her when she was nine years old.

However, the inclusion in Surat al-Baqarah of rulings on Hajj and ʿUmrah and rulings on fighting the polytheists in the sacred month and the sacred city indicates that its revelation continued until the year five and the year six, as we will explain at the verse ﴿But if you are prevented, then (send) what offering is feasible﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

[Page 202]

It may have extended to after the year eight, as His words imply: ﴿The pilgrimage is in known months﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], and the verses up to His words ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203]. It has been said that His words ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281] are the last thing revealed of the Qur'an. We have explained in the Eighth Introduction that the revelation of a surah may continue, so other surahs are revealed during the period of its revelation.

Surat al-Baqarah is counted as the eighty-seventh in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Mutaffifin and before Al ʿImran.

Since the revelation of this surah was at the very beginning of the establishment of the Islamic community (al-jami'ah al-islamiyyah) and the independence of the people of Islam in their city, one of the first aims of this surah was to purify the Islamic community from being mixed with corrupting elements, in order to preserve the goodness God established for it, striving to form the virtuous and pure city, free from the impurities of deception and corruption.

Since it was the first surah revealed after the Hijrah, it was cared for by the Ansar, who devoted themselves to memorizing it. This is shown by what came in the biography (al-sirah) that: "When the Muslims were routed on the day of Hunayn, the Prophet ﷺ said to al-ʿAbbas: 'Shout, O company of the Ansar, O people of the tree (al-samurah),' meaning the tree of the pledge at al-Hudaybiyah, 'O people of Surat al-Baqarah!' So the Ansar said: 'At your service, at your service, O Messenger of God! Rejoice!'"

In the Muwatta', Malik said: "It reached me that ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar remained on Surat al-Baqarah for eight years, learning it." In Sahih al-Bukhari: "There was a Christian who embraced Islam and read al-Baqarah and Al ʿImran, and he used to write for the Prophet ﷺ, then he apostatized..." to the end of the story.

The number of its verses is two hundred and eighty-five according to the counters of Medina, Mecca and Syria; two hundred and eighty-six according to the counters of Kufa; and two hundred and eighty-seven according to the counters of Basra.

This surah has far-reaching aspects, and its methods are many-branched. It has gathered from the threads of the aims of the surahs what was a true confirmation of its title "the tent of the Qur'an." One cannot count its contents by reckoning, and the reader should look forward to the details of some of them in what will come of our commentary. But this does not hold us back from touching upon some glimpses of them. They have been woven with the weaving of the contextual links (al-munasabat) and the rhetorical considerations, a firm warp in the structure of the speech, and a solid woof of the eloquence of words.

Most of its aims divide into two parts: one part establishes the sublimity of this religion over what preceded it, the exaltedness of its guidance, and its principles for purifying souls; and the other part explains the laws of this religion for its followers and the reform of their society.

Its style is the best of styles that can be: a style that combines the excellences of oratorical styles, the styles of legislative books, and the styles of admonition and exhortation. With such a style the energy of the listeners is renewed, through the variety of its arts. It is evident to us from its aims that it opened with an allusion to the challenge to the obstinate Arabs, a general challenge, through the disjoined letters with which it opens, a symbol that calls for their anticipation of what follows it and their waiting to learn its purpose. Then it followed with praise of the Qur'an, so the symbol turned into an indication of part of the purpose of that symbol, which has the strongest impact upon their souls, and they remain awaiting what follows it of explicit challenge, which will come after His words ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23] and the verses that follow. He then turned them toward praise of the excellent truthfulness of this Book and its guidance. He passed on to classifying people, with respect to their reception of this Book and their benefit from its guidance, into four categories (before the Hijrah there were two), according to the differences in their states in that reception.

Since the category most benefiting from its guidance were those who believe in the unseen and establish the prayer, meaning the Muslims, it began by mentioning them. And since the most stubborn and rancorous categories were the open polytheists and the hypocrites, the two groups were treated together as one and were admonished with decisive proofs and clear evidences. Then it gave special length to the category of the hypocrites, to expose their hypocrisy, to declare their inner intentions, and to refute their criticisms. Then the conclusion of what struck their noses was the explicit challenge that it had symbolized at the beginning, a challenge that forces them into submission and silences their tongues from insolence and eloquence, and casts into the depths of their souls the humiliation of defeat and the truthfulness of the Messenger who challenged them. This was of the type of "returning the last part to the first" (radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-sadr), so the scope became wide for calling the fair-minded to worship the true Lord who created them and created the heavens and the earth, and who bestowed upon them what is in the earth entirely.

It passed on to the description of the beginning of the creation of man, for in that there is a reminder to them of the first creation before their idols came into being, the idols they claim were the righteous of the people of Noah and those after them. And it is a favor upon the species in preferring their origin over the creatures of this world, and in their distinction of knowing what the exalted assembly (al-malaʾ al-aʿla) did not know, and how the enmity of Satan toward him and his offspring arose. This is to prepare the souls of the listeners to suspect their desires and to hold themselves accountable for their claims.

This favour, which encompassed all four categories mentioned above, was a fitting transition to a great favour specifically concerning the fourth group, the People of the Book (*ahl al-kitab*), who are the most resistant of all people to the guidance of the Qur'an and the most influential of the groups over the common Arabs. This is because the People of the Book were, at that time, the people of knowledge and the ones the common folk were most likely to follow. This is seen in His words, ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:40), and the verses that follow. He elaborated at length in reminding them of Allah's favours and His days toward them, and described what they had met with in return for His abundant favours: deviation from the upright path, a deviation that reached the point of disbelief. This comprises the essence of the formation of the Children of Israel as a nation and their unification in the time of Musa (Moses). Then came the most important of their events with the prophets who followed Musa, until they received the call of Islam with envy and hostility, even toward the angel Jibril (Gabriel). The verses also explain their errors, because this casts doubt in people's souls on their fitness to be followed. He mentioned from this a model of their character: their attachment to life, ﴿And you will surely find them the most avid of people for life﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:96); their attempt to practise sorcery, ﴿and they followed what the devils recited﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:102), and so on; and their harming of the Prophet through direct speech, ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:104). Then the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists were joined together in one envy of the Muslims and their anger at the new law: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not wish that any good be sent down upon you﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:105), up to His words, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:112). Then came the dispute that arose between the Jews and the Christians, and each group's claim that it alone was in the right: ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians are not based on anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not based on anything"﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:113), up to His words, ﴿they dispute﴾. Then the polytheists were singled out as the greatest wrongdoers among these three categories, because they prevented the Muslims from remembering Allah in the Sacred Mosque and strove in that to ruin it. They resembled the Jews and the Christians in this and united with them in their hatred of Islam.

He then moved, by way of this connection, to the virtues of the Sacred Mosque, its builder, and his supplication for his descendants for guidance, and to the caution against responding to it by those among them who disbelieved. He also (mentioned) that Islam is founded on the creed of Ibrahim (Abraham), which is monotheism, and that Judaism and Christianity are not the creed of Ibrahim. From this is the return to facing the Ka'bah (*qiblah*), which Allah reserved for the Muslims as a sign that Islam is the religion established on the upright monotheistic faith (*al-hanifiyyah*). He also mentioned the rites of Allah in Makkah, and silenced the People of the Book in their criticism of the change of the *qiblah*. He (further explained) that caring for the purification of souls is more worthy than caring for the direction one faces: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:177). They were reminded of the abrogation (*naskh*, the replacement of one ruling by a later one) of laws for the benefit of nations, and that there is no novelty in abrogating the law of the Torah or the Gospel by what is better than them both.

Then he returned to disputing with the polytheists by using as evidence the signs of Allah's handiwork: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, and the ship﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:164), and so on. (He also disputed with) the polytheists on a day when they will disown their leaders. He refuted the claims of both groups' religions concerning forbidden foods: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:172). He completed this by mentioning a small category of people, namely the polytheists who did not manifest Islam but displayed affection for the Muslims: ﴿And among people is one whose speech in the worldly life pleases you﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:204). When he had fulfilled the full right of all this with the most wondrous clarification and the clearest proof, he moved to the category of Islamic legislation in summary, with His words, ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:177), and then in detail: retribution (*qisas*), bequest, fasting, retreat (*i'tikaf*), pilgrimage, jihad, the system of social conduct and the family, financial transactions, spending in the way of Allah, charity, intoxicants, orphans, inheritance, sales and usury, debts, witnessing, pledges, marriage, the rulings on women, the waiting period (*'iddah*), divorce, breastfeeding, maintenance, and oaths.

The surah concluded with a supplication that includes the distinctive features of the Islamic law, and this is among the comprehensive utterances (*jawami' al-kalim*). This conclusion was thus a summary and a recapitulation: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And whether you disclose what is within yourselves or conceal it﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:284), and the verses that follow.

Throughout all of this there were various aims, which came earlier in digressions amid scattered occasions, renewing the energy of the reader and the listener, just as the face of the sun shines forth after the falling of abundant rains, and the first buds of flowers emerge after the crashing thunder. These aims include: the glorification of Allah and His attributes, ﴿Allah — there is no deity except Him﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:255); His mercy and the tolerance of Islam; the coining of parables, such as "or like a rain-cloud" (Al-Baqarah 2:19), and the evoking of analogies, ﴿And indeed among stones﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:74); ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:243); knowledge and wisdom; the meanings of faith and Islam; the strengthening of the Muslims, ﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:153); the fundamental perfections and the embellishing virtues; the taking of deeds and meanings from their realities and benefits rather than from their outward forms; and not regarding technical terms when they do not aim at ends: ﴿It is not righteousness to enter the houses from their backs﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:189), ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:177), and ﴿and expelling its people from it is greater in the sight of Allah﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:217). They also include reflection and reasoning, the system of argumentation, the reports of past nations, the messengers and their relative excellence, and the diversity of laws.
